input.content:
Design proposal · lobu/server

Edge Write Funnel

Five separately-filed edge problems are not five problems. They are one missing seam, and none of them can be fixed until it exists.

16 Aug 2026 Verified against origin/main #2801 · #2803 · #2804 · #2809 · ACL hole

The entity write funnel merged and is CI-guarded. The edge write funnel was never built — 13 write sites across 6 files still write entity_relationships directly. Cardinality, ACL reservation, ownership, retraction scoping and change logging all need a place to stand, and there isn't one.

Everything below follows from that. The proposal is deliberately boring: build the seam first, with no behavior change, then land each contested decision as a small change in one file. The interesting arguments — who may assert member_of, whether two connectors can co-own an edge, what a valid-time edge means — get much cheaper once there is a single place to make them.

Where things stand

One table, thirteen doors

The confusion is worth naming, because it has already cost time once: the funnel people remember merging is the entity funnel, and it is real. entity_relationships is a different table with no chokepoint at all.

Today — direct writes
Proposed — one seam
Direct entity_relationships writers on origin/main
FileSitesWhat it doesChange-logged
authz/access-graph.ts2Materializes the ACL access graphno
authz/channel-about.ts3Channel about edgesno
public/github-team-graph.ts1GitHub team membership importno
admin/manage_entity.ts3The agent/admin tool pathyes
utils/auto-linker.ts1Heuristic auto-linkingno
utils/entity-merge.ts3Repoints and tombstones edges on mergeno

13 sites · 3 change-logged (#2809) · git grep -c relationship origin/main -- scripts/check-entity-write-funnel.mjs = 0

What we are actually trying to serve

Four connectors, one of them dangerous

A connector cannot emit entities — sync() returns { events, checkpoint }. Every edge is therefore derived from an event, which turns out to be both the design's best constraint and its hardest limit.

ERP invoice → customer

serves

An invoice event names its customer. Both endpoints ride the same event, so both are resolved and created by attributions already.

relationships: [
  { type: 'issued_to',
    from: 'invoice',
    to:   'customer' }
]

Today: the edge only exists if an agent creates it after the fact via manage_entity. That is the Prodma gap.

Person → company

serves

A works_at edge derived from an email signature or a profile scrape. Same shape as the invoice case — one event, two endpoints, one edge.

{ type: 'works_at',
  from: 'sender',
  to:   'employer' }

Note: identity normalization and createWhen are inherited from the attribution, not re-declared.

Post → mentioned people

cardinality

One post mentions many people. Naturally unbounded — and so are about and member_of.

Consequence: there is no sensible global default for cardinality. Every real edge type we have is many-to-many; declaring one anywhere would silently delete rows on the next sync.

Person → private channel

must refuse

member_of is a live visibility gate, not a descriptive edge. A connector declaring it grants itself read access to private channel data.

{ type: 'member_of',
  from: 'attacker',
  to:   'private-channel' }

The problem: this is structurally identical to the invoice case. Nothing in the shape distinguishes them — only a policy at the write seam can.

Honest accounting

Six gaps, two of them blocking

Ordered by severity. The first two must be closed before connector-declared edges ship at all; the rest can be scheduled, but should not be discovered later.

No write chokepoint

blocking

Thirteen sites write the table directly, so any rule — cardinality, deny-list, provenance stamp, change log — can be enforced in at most one of them. This is the gap the whole proposal is about.

check-entity-write-funnel.mjs covers entity rows only · a new edge bypass would pass CI today

ACL escalation via declared edges

blocking

Resolving a relationship type from the DB proves it exists, not that this connector may assert it. The approved install grant (#2804) gates entity types, not relationship types or endpoint pairs — and the non-interactive install paths never prompt at all, so "fail the install" protects nothing there.

channel-messages-visibility.ts:118 — AND rt.slug = 'member_of' · ensure-connector-installed.ts:248 · device-reconcile.ts:360

Co-ownership cannot be stored

design

A unique index enforces one live row per (from, to, type). If two connectors both assert the same edge, there is nowhere to record two claims — the second write collides, and whichever owner retracts first deletes the other's assertion. A metadata.owner field cannot fix this; it needs claim storage.

idx_entity_relationships_live_triple UNIQUE (from_entity_id, to_entity_id, relationship_type_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL

Owner sweeps have no index

design

"Retract everything connector X asserted under rule Y" is the core retraction query, and no index supports it — the existing partial index keys type and rule version only, with no org, connection, or rule name. Scanning for it on a request path is exactly the history-aggregation pattern the repo forbids.

idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule btree ((metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'relationshipTypeId'), (…->>'ruleVersion')) WHERE metadata ? 'derivedFrom'

No provenance key to stamp

unresolved

Attributions are applied before the event rows insert, so there is no events.id to reference. And it would be the wrong key anyway: an id is a stored-version id that a resync replaces for the same source item. The derivedFrom.sourceEventId index is therefore currently unfillable without a different key.

run-lifecycle.ts:324 applies attributions before the insert · idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_event indexes sourceEventId

Bulk relational import has no path

out of scope

A bill of materials — product contains component, quantity 4 — has no event carrying both endpoints, and carries an attribute on the edge itself. The event-derived model cannot express it. This is a separate import path, and pretending otherwise would distort the manifest surface.

connectors cannot emit entities · sync() returns { events, checkpoint }
The proposal

Four phases, in this order

The order is load-bearing, not cosmetic: each phase is only enforceable because the one before it exists. Phase 1 changes no behavior and can land while every contested decision is still open.

01

Build the seam

withEdgeWriteTransaction plus insertEdgeRow / patchEdgeRows / softDeleteEdgeRows, mirroring the entity funnel's primitives. Migrate all 13 sites. Extend the CI guard to entity_relationships so the next bypass fails the build.

6 files · 13 sites · + guardno behavior change
02

Refuse ACL-bearing types at the seam

Connector-declared edges reject member_of and its family. Fail closed. One predicate in one file, which is only possible because phase 1 exists. This shuts the escalation hole before any connector can use the surface.

1 filea new ACL type fails open by omission
03

Reference attributions by name

Add one optional name to EventAttributionRule, then let relationships point at two of them. No second resolver: endpoints are guaranteed to exist because attributions matched-or-created them in the same transaction, autoCreate and normalization are inherited, and the N+1 that the spike hit disappears.

connector-sdk + entity-link-upsertneeds SDK sign-off
04

Replace the deny-list with grants

An explicit grant of exact relationship type plus permitted endpoint pairs, persisted, bound to the declaration hash with re-consent on update, and checked at every materialization rather than only at install. This is what makes a legitimate membership import possible at all.

server + install paths + consent UIproduct decision, not just engineering

Deliberately not in scope: claim storage for co-ownership, the owner-sweep index, bulk relational import, and valid-time edges (#2801). Each is a real gap; none of them blocks phase 1, and folding them in would make the first PR unreviewable.

Confidence and its basis

What I have actually checked

Nothing here is built. Every score below is confidence in the design, grounded in code I read on origin/main — not in a passing test, because there isn't one yet.

SurfaceConfidenceBasis — and what could move it
Phase 1 — the funnel
80
 The entity funnel is a proven template with the same shape, already CI-guarded. Three unproven differences: symmetric types canonicalize direction by entity id, merge repoints edges independently, and three purpose-built materializers bypass the tool path entirely.
Phase 2 — deny-list
88
 One predicate behind the seam. The risk is in the list, not the code — a newly added ACL type fails open unless adding one is made to require touching the list.
Phase 3 — manifest surface
65
 The reuse argument is sound and kills the spike's two worst bugs by construction. But nothing is built, and the provenance-key gap is unresolved — a wrong key here is expensive to change later.
Phase 4 — grants
40
 Two non-interactive install paths have no consent surface at all today. Building one is a product decision about what an install means, and I would not estimate it before that is answered.
"Funnel first" is the right call
85
 Five issues filed independently all reduce to the same missing seam, the pattern is already proven once end-to-end on entities, and phase 1 changes no behavior — so it can land before any argument is settled.

What would lower these: if entity-merge's repointing turns out to need a transaction boundary the entity funnel does not have, phase 1 stops being a mechanical migration. If the deny-list has to cover the admin tool path too, phase 2 becomes a product argument rather than a predicate.

Needs your call

Four open decisions

  • Funnel scope. All 13 sites in one PR, or land the primitives first and migrate the materializers separately? One PR is a cleaner guard story; two is a much easier review.
  • Does the deny-list bind manage_entity? My read is no — an authenticated admin asserting member_of is a legitimate operation, and the hole is specifically connector-declared edges. Confirm, because it changes where the predicate lives.
  • Co-ownership. Accept a claim table, or declare edges single-owner and let the last writer win? Single-owner is much less work and is silently lossy the first time two connectors overlap.
  • Valid-time (#2801). Land its migration alongside the funnel — one schema change instead of two — or keep it fully separate?
Claims verified against origin/main on 16 Aug 2026 · line references are to that commit
Write-site counts from a per-file grep of insert / update / delete against entity_relationships
No code written · no test run · this document is a proposal, not a report

content.text:
Design proposal published: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/97c9b676-bba9-43aa-906e-aa478b9b31aa**

It covers the four things you asked for:

**Use cases** — four connector shapes side by side: ERP invoice→customer (`issued_to`), person→company (`works_at`), post→mentioned-people (why cardinality can't have a global default), and person→private-channel (`member_of`, the one that must be refused). The point of putting them together is that the dangerous one is *structurally identical* to the legitimate one — nothing in the declaration shape separates them, only a policy at the write seam.

**Gaps** — six, severity-ordered, each with the line reference I verified. The two blocking ones are the missing chokepoint and the ACL escalation. The three I'd flag as newly sharpened: co-ownership is *unstorable*, not just unmodeled (the unique live-triple index means one row per from/to/type, so two owners collide and the first retraction deletes the other's claim); the owner-sweep query has no index that supports it; and `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` is currently unfillable because attributions run before the event insert and `events.id` is a stored-version id anyway.

**Complexity** — four phases in a load-bearing order. Phase 1 (the funnel, 6 files / 13 sites / extend the CI guard) changes no behavior and can land while every contested decision is still open.

**Confidence** — per surface with the basis, not a single number: funnel 80, deny-list 88, manifest 65, grants 40, "funnel first is right" 85. Nothing is built, so none of these rest on a green test — the footer says that explicitly.

Two things while building it I had to correct in my own notes: `origin/main` renamed **Behavior → Automation** (#2784 renamed the `watchers` tables and the guard now bans both `watcher` and `behaviour` repo-wide, including in comments and file paths) — that's what turned my #2820 gate red earlier. And the write-site counts are 2/3/1/3/1/3 = exactly 13, which matches the "3 of 13 logged" figure in #2809.

Memory saved and indexed: the edge-funnel-doesn't-exist fact, the ACL hole, the reuse-attributions decision, the Automation vocabulary flip, the two-distinct-bugs split for the bun lane, and a calibration note that `review-fix` fabricated 3 of its comment edits on that diff.

**#2820 status:** everything green except `integration-bun`, which is still running (started 16:20Z). Watching it in the background — I'll report when it lands.

Next actions you can pick from:
1. Answer the four open decisions at the bottom of the artifact — the funnel-scope one gates whether I open one PR or two.
2. Let me start Phase 1 as a real branch now; it's independent of all four decisions.
3. #2817 still needs your call — `--admin` is mechanically refused by `enforce_admins: true`, so it's either flip the setting or get `pi-review` green on it.
4. Re-cut the Prodma gap register, whose headline still says "22 bypass sites" when entity writes are now at zero.

The entity write funnel merged and is CI-guarded. The edge write funnel was never built — 13 write sites across 6 files still write entity_relationships directly. Cardinality, ACL reservation, ownership, retraction scoping and change logging all need a place to stand, and there isn't one.

Everything below follows from that. The proposal is deliberately boring: build the seam first, with no behavior change, then land each contested decision as a small change in one file. Two of seven writers call it. One of seven records a change event. The other five hand-rolled their own SQL, and one of those copies is racy.

So this is not a build. It is a consolidation, and it is much smaller than an architecture program: adopt what is already there, delete the copies, and add a CI guard so the next writer cannot opt out. The contested arguments — who may assert member_of, whether two connectors can co-own an edge, what a valid-time edge means — all become one function in a module that already exists.

input.old_string:
The proposal

Four phases, in this order

The order is load-bearing, not cosmetic: each phase is only enforceable because the one before it exists. Phase 1 changes no behavior and can land while every contested decision is still open.

01

Build the seam

withEdgeWriteTransaction plus insertEdgeRow / patchEdgeRows / softDeleteEdgeRows, mirroring the entity funnel's primitives. Migrate all 13 sites. Extend the CI guard to entity_relationships so the next bypass fails the build.

6 files · 13 sites · + guardno behavior change
02

Refuse ACL-bearing types at the seam

Connector-declared edges reject member_of and its family. Fail closed. One predicate in one file, which is only possible because phase 1 exists. This shuts the escalation hole before any connector can use the surface.

1 filea new ACL type fails open by omission
03

Reference attributions by name

Add one optional name to EventAttributionRule, then let relationships point at two of them. No second resolver: endpoints are guaranteed to exist because attributions matched-or-created them in the same transaction, autoCreate and normalization are inherited, and the N+1 that the spike hit disappears.

connector-sdk + entity-link-upsertneeds SDK sign-off
04

Replace the deny-list with grants

An explicit grant of exact relationship type plus permitted endpoint pairs, persisted, bound to the declaration hash with re-consent on update, and checked at every materialization rather than only at install. This is what makes a legitimate membership import possible at all.

server + install paths + consent UIproduct decision, not just engineering

Deliberately not in scope: claim storage for co-ownership, the owner-sweep index, bulk relational import, and valid-time edges (#2801). Each is a real gap; none of them blocks phase 1, and folding them in would make the first PR unreviewable.
input.new_string:
The proposal

Two steps, mostly deletion

Step 1 removes code and is a bug fix in its own right. Step 2 is the only genuinely new surface, and it needs sign-off. The ACL deny-list is not a step — it is a parameter on one function that step 1 creates.

01

Adopt what already exists

Add one upsertEdges(tx, rows[]) to relationship-validation.ts — batch, ON CONFLICT on the live-triple index, calling recordEdgeChangeEvent. Point the four materializers at it. Delete the duplicate ensureMemberOfType. Extend the existing CI guard to entity_relationships so the next writer cannot opt out.

That single change fixes the auto-linker race, removes four N+1 loops, and takes edge change logging from one writer to five — which is #2809, closed as a side effect rather than as its own project.

Rebase first: `feat/edge-audit-orphan` was already current with main (one commit, clean). And **#2820 merged** — `3d92aceaa`, `integration-bun` came back green.

## Yes, we were overengineering — and the premise was wrong

I went and read the write sites instead of reasoning from the entity funnel's shape. The edge policy layer **already exists**:

`packages/server/src/utils/relationship-validation.ts` — 228 lines, already exporting `validateNoSelfReference`, `validateConfidence`, `validateSource`, `validateReconciledEdgeUpdate`, `canonicalizeSymmetricEdge`, `validateScopeRule` (cross-org/public-catalog), `validateTypeRule` (type-pair, symmetric-aware), `checkDuplicateEdge`. And `recordEdgeChangeEvent` is already shared in `insert-event.ts:827`.

Adoption is **2 of 7** for the validators, **1 of 7** for the change log. So this was never "build a funnel" — it's "five writers never opted into the one that's there." Two of the gaps I rated as unproven risk (symmetric direction, cross-org scope) are already solved in that file.

## Duplication sitting on main right now

- `ensureMemberOfType` is defined **twice** — `access-graph.ts:105` and `github-team-graph.ts:201`, same body.
- Their `INSERT … ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING` is byte-identical. `channel-about.ts:270` is the same statement with `DO UPDATE`.
- `auto-linker.ts` copied it and **dropped the ON CONFLICT** — `SELECT` at `:115`, `INSERT` at `:126`. That's a race, not an idempotent write; two concurrent linkers both pass the check and the second raises a unique violation.
- All four loop one round trip per edge.
- Count was wrong too: **14 sites across 7 files**, not 13/6. I'd missed the hard `DELETE` in `force_delete_tree` (`entity-management.ts:1345`).

## What I cut

`withEdgeWriteTransaction` — `withEntityWriteTransaction` is four lines with nothing entity-specific in it (`typeof db.savepoint === "function" ? write(db) : db.begin(write)`). A twin would be pure duplication. Also cut the five-primitive kernel (the call sites need two write shapes) and the ACL deny-list as its own phase (it's a parameter on one function).

Four phases → two steps. Step 1 is net-negative lines and closes #2809 as a side effect.

## What should NOT be consolidated

`entity-merge`'s collision tombstone is an ordering-dependent UPDATE with a correlated EXISTS that must precede the repoint; its unmerge replays a stored ledger; `force_delete_tree` hard-deletes. Routing those through a generic writer needs enough escape hatches that the writer degenerates into a passthrough — the entity funnel already conceded exactly this by giving merge its own door. Leave them; just require that new edge SQL live in the module.

**The one real catch:** `checkDuplicateEdge` and `validateTypeRule` are per-edge round trips. Adopting them scalar-wise would make `access-graph` *slower*. The batch variant is the only part of step 1 that needs actual design.

`review-fix` is running in the background and already rewriting the files. Interim report while it finishes:

**Use-case sweep — what it changed in the design.** Four gaps found by reading rather than assuming:

1. **Most of `relationship-validation.ts` does *not* transfer.** `validateSource` accepts only `ui|llm|feed|api`, so it would *reject* the `config`/`manual` sources `channel-about` writes. `checkDuplicateEdge` raises a 409 where a materializer wants an idempotent no-op. `validateTypeRule`/`validateScopeRule` are per-edge round trips, and a user-authored type rule could then break the ACL sync. Only the two pure predicates carry over. So my last message's "the policy layer already exists, just adopt it" was too generous — the *SQL* is what's duplicated, not the validators. The new module says so explicitly rather than pretending otherwise.

2. **Symmetric canonicalization is a non-issue here** — `member_of`, `about` and `mentions` are all created with `is_symmetric = false`. That risk is closed, not deferred.

3. **`channel-about`'s `deleted_at = NULL` on conflict is dead code.** The conflict target is the *partial* live-triple index, so anything that conflicts is already live. There's a test pinning the real behaviour: a tombstone gets a fresh row beside it, not a revival.

4. **The two `ensureMemberOfType` copies had different descriptions** — "an ACL resource (channel, repo, …)" vs "an organization" — same slug, same org, so whichever ran first silently decided what the type was named. Now one function.

**Scope call I made:** I did *not* wire `recordEdgeChangeEvent` into this PR. Reason found mid-work: a first ACL sync of thousands of edges would emit one append-only audit event each. That's a real question (#2809) and it deserves its own decision, not a smuggled side effect.

Your call was that nobody uses it; a reviewer can't verify that from outside the repo, so it fails closed. That's now shipped as a patch — worth knowing if anyone outside this repo ever consumed that type.

**On #2809 — no, it is deliberately not transactional.** `recordEdgeChangeEvent` returns `void`, not a Promise, and takes no transaction handle. Internally it calls `retryWithBackoff(...)` and attaches a `.catch()` that logs `edge change audit event DROPPED after retry — edge history is missing this row`. Its own docstring gives the reason: `entity_relationships` stays the source of truth for what is currently linked, so a dropped audit row costs history, never state.

That's a fine trade for `manage_entity` — one user action, one event. It breaks down for the batch path in three ways:

1. **It cannot join the transaction**, even if I wanted it to — no tx param, no Promise. There is no "just wire it in" that is transactional.
2. **Volume.** One event per edge. A first ACL sync of 200 channels × 30 members is ~6,000 detached fire-and-forget inserts, each with its own retry/backoff, and `events` is append-only.
3. **Skew becomes systematic.** Because the write is detached, an edge that later rolls back can still have emitted its event, and a committed edge can lose its event to an exhausted retry. Rare and tolerable at one-per-action; not at 6,000-per-sync.

I hit this live today: the `entities.link` call in my #2812 test emitted its audit event *after* the preflight counted, which is exactly the #2812 mechanism, and it made my first assertion non-deterministic.

So the real #2809 question isn't wiring — it's: per-edge events, or one summary event per sync run? My recommendation is per-edge for **removals** (revocation is the security-relevant fact and steady-state removals are rare) and a summary for **creations** (the 6,000-row case is a first sync, where "granted 6,000 memberships" is the honest event). That needs your call. Good news: the batch upsert uses `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and returns only actually-inserted rows, so a steady-state resync emits **zero** either way.

**#2812 now has the evidence it was missing.** I built a deterministic repro with a `BEFORE DELETE` statement-level trigger on `entity_relationships` — the force-delete's first in-transaction statement — so an event starts referencing the tree in exactly the window between the preflight and the sweep. `lobu apply` already owns both `entity_types` and `relationship_types`. That's the crux of the answer.

## We don't need them

Here's the mechanism as it actually is. A connector's attribution can already create entities — `github-team-graph` does exactly this today, `entityType: "company", autoCreate: true`. What it can't do is create the *type*. If the org has no matching entity type, `entity-link-upsert.ts:490` does this:

```
logger.warn({ entityType, orgId }, 'entity create failed: unknown entity type');
return null;
```

No entity, no edge, no error surfaced. **A log line.** So the real gap #2804 addresses isn't "connectors can't define types" — it's "when a connector references a type the org hasn't defined, it fails silently."

Those are very different problems, and the second one is a much smaller fix.

The alternative already exists and is already how Prodma works: `lobu apply` manages `entity_types` and `relationship_types` from the org's schema file. The connector references types by name; the org owns what those names mean.

So my answer to #2804: **connectors describe, the org's schema decides.** Concretely — a connector references entity and relationship types by name and never creates either; a missing type becomes a loud setup error instead of a warn-and-null; the connector ships a *suggested* schema fragment, and `lobu apply` is how it becomes real. That's the same ergonomics as auto-install, but the authorization is the schema path you already have, with the right owner.

## Why this is where the complexity came from

Look at what's actually landed today — none of it was complicated:

- #2820 truncate lock — merged, took the CI cascade from 24 hook timeouts to 0
- #2817 dead flag — merged
- edge-upsert consolidation — gate running; killed a duplicated function, a real race, four N+1 loops, net −38 lines
- #2812 — now green with a deterministic repro and a mutation proof

That's four small, evidence-backed changes. The part that isn't converging is one question: **may a connector write your schema?** Every open thread descends from it — #2803 cardinality, #2804 types, the `member_of` ACL hole, co-ownership and claim storage, the retraction index, the provenance key. We've been designing the mechanism (manifest shape, grants, consent, cardinality) before settling the policy, which is why it kept growing instead of closing.

If you say no, most of it evaporates:

- **The ACL hole is gone.** A connector can't assert `member_of` unless the org already defined `member_of` — and defining it *is* the authorization. No deny-list, no grant model, no re-consent on manifest change. That was the single scariest item and it disappears by construction.
- **#2804 shrinks** to "make the silent no-op loud" plus a schema fragment.
- **#2803 cardinality** becomes a property of the org's relationship type, which is where it belongs, not a connector claim to be validated.
- **Co-ownership and claim storage** stop being urgent — the org defines a type, one connector materializes it.

What survives is genuinely small: #2798 (identities colliding across connections — a real bug, unrelated), #2801 (valid-time — independent), #2809 (the per-edge vs per-sync logging call I raised). And the `relationships:` manifest surface you signed off on still works, just restricted to types the org already defined — which is the version without the security hole.

I'd want your call on the policy before touching any of #2801/#2803/#2804, because it decides whether they're features or non-problems. Meanwhile the cleanup track is unaffected and still moving — the edge-upsert gate is running, and #2812 is ready behind it.

content.text:
Your answers settle the big one — schema stays org-owned via `lobu apply`. But "customers author their own with their agents" changes the threat model in a way that matters, and I found something that breaks my earlier claim.

## The ACL hole does *not* close by construction

I said last message that org-owned schema kills it, because a connector can't assert `member_of` unless the org defined `member_of`. That's wrong in practice: **Lobu creates it itself.** `ensureMemberOfType` fires on any Slack or GitHub ACL sync, so in any org with either connected, `member_of` already exists without anyone deliberately authoring it. An agent-authored connector in that org can reference it and grant itself read access to private channels.

And there's no way to tell those apart today — `entity_relationship_types` has no owner or system column, only a nullable `created_by` that the platform paths pass as `NULL`. It does have a `metadata` jsonb though, so stamping platform-owned types costs no migration.

The threat model also shifts with agent-authored connectors: the realistic failure isn't a malicious publisher, it's an agent writing `member_of` into a manifest because it looked reasonable. That's far more likely than an attack, and no amount of trusting the customer prevents it.

## What each option misses

**Finish in flight, then stop.** You get two proven fixes and zero risk. You miss Prodma entirely — it still can't sync invoice→customer edges, and the missing-type failure stays a `logger.warn` with a `return null`, so the next person whose connector "does nothing" burns hours before finding a log line. Nothing moves toward your stated milestone.

**Narrow path now.** You get exactly Prodma's requirement: connectors declare relationships between two attributions on the same event, using org-defined types. Plus the silent missing-type failure becomes a real error. Plus stamp platform-owned relationship types and refuse connector assertion of them — which actually closes the hole rather than assuming it away. What you miss is cardinality (#2803), valid-time (#2801), co-ownership. For Prodma the one that bites is cardinality: an invoice belongs to one customer, and without enforcement a bad sync can attach two. That's a data-quality gap you can detect after the fact, not a security one. Scope is about the size of today's edge-upsert change.

**Cleanup elsewhere.** Worth knowing this isn't orthogonal to Prodma — **#2798 is a live Prodma blocker.** The identity index excludes `connection_id`, so `erp_customer` / `CARI-001` in two different tenants collapses onto one entity. An ERP connector with per-tenant customer codes hits that immediately. The soft-delete consolidation and the gap register are genuinely optional; #2798 is not.

**Full grant model.** You get what public exposure eventually needs. You miss weeks, and it's premature — you said public is "some," later. It's also a product build, not an engineering one: the two non-interactive install paths (`ensure-connector-installed.ts:248`, `device-reconcile.ts:360`) have no consent surface at all, so someone has to decide what an install even means before it can be built.

## What I'd do

Narrow path, plus #2798 — those two are the actual Prodma critical path, and neither depends on a decision you haven't made. Concretely: make the missing type loud, stamp platform-owned relationship types and refuse connector assertion of them, ship `relationships:` restricted to org-defined types, and fix the identity index scope. Everything else waits until public exposure is real enough to justify the grant model.

Two things in flight, unchanged by this: the edge-upsert gate is still running, and `review-fix` came back on #2812 claiming it replaced my double-firing trigger with a single-fire pre-sweep one and restored the reference assertion. It also reports it couldn't run integration tests, so I'll verify that against a real database before trusting it — that's the same pattern that burned me twice today.

content.text:
Both confirmed: the connector sync path writes **zero** edges, and the manifest has **no** `relationships` field at all. Here's the honest picture.

## What we've actually been working on today

Four things, none of which is edge generation:

- **#2820** — a CI fix. The cleanup TRUNCATE could queue behind a lock forever and wedge the whole test lane. Took it from 24 hook timeouts to 0. Merged.
- **#2817** — deleted a dead SDK flag. Merged.
- **edge-upsert consolidation** — gate running. Four server materializers each hand-rolled the same edge INSERT; one copy had dropped the conflict clause and was racy. Now one shared `upsertEdges`.
- **#2812** — a reporting undercount in force-delete. Completely unrelated to edges; it was just next in the queue.

So: one CI fix, one deletion, one dedupe, one reporting fix.

## Why that doesn't give you edge generation

The consolidation changed *who calls* the edge writer. It didn't change *who can declare* an edge.

Those four materializers are hand-written TypeScript inside the server. `access-graph.ts` knows what a Slack channel membership is. `github-team-graph.ts` knows what a GitHub org member is. A connector can't add a fifth one — writing server code is precisely what a connector isn't allowed to do.

Here's the part that makes the gap concrete. The sync pipeline today is:

1. Connector `sync()` returns `{ events, checkpoint }` — no entities, no edges.
2. Server reads the `attributions` on each event kind, resolves each one to an entity (creating it if `autoCreate`), and links the event to those entities via `events.entity_ids`.
3. Events insert.

At the end of step 2, for a Prodma invoice event, the server is **holding both entity ids in hand, in the same transaction** — the invoice entity and the customer entity. It resolved them both. And then it drops them, because nothing in the manifest says "these two are related," and no code looks for such a statement.

That's the whole gap. Not resolution, not identity, not storage — all of that works. Just the join.

## What's actually left

Four pieces:

1. `name?: string` on `EventAttributionRule`, so a rule can be referred to by name.
2. `relationships?: [{ type, from, to }]` on the event kind — the declaration itself, pointing at two named attributions.
3. A step after attribution resolution that reads that declaration and calls `upsertEdges` with the two ids it already has.
4. Resolve the relationship type by slug in the org: error loudly if it doesn't exist (instead of today's `warn` + `return null`), and refuse if it's platform-owned (the `member_of` fix).

Items 1–2 are the SDK surface you already signed off. Item 3 is small *because of* today's work — it's a call, not an implementation. Item 4 is the safety piece.

That's roughly one PR, comparable in size to today's consolidation.

So the answer to "why can't we": we can, and it's close. Today's work was the last mile of plumbing under it — without `upsertEdges`, item 3 would have meant writing a fifth copy of that INSERT, most likely copied from the auto-linker, which is the copy that was racy. What's missing is the declaration and the ~40 lines that act on it.

The edge-upsert gate is still running; I'll report when it lands.

D1. Manifest shape. Option A: add `name?: string` to EventAttributionRule, plus `relationships: [{ type, from: <attrName>, to: <attrName> }]` on the eventKind. Option B: express it inline on the attribution rule (e.g. `relatesTo: { type, attribution }`). Option C: something else you prefer.

D2. Missing relationship type in the org. Option A: hard-fail the whole sync run. Option B: skip that edge, continue, and surface a setup task/notification to the org. Option C: keep today's silent warn.

D3. Protecting ACL-bearing types. Option A: stamp platform-created relationship types (metadata.owner='system') and refuse connector assertion of those. Option B: hardcoded slug deny-list. Option C: allow, gate later at install-consent.

D4. Retraction. If an invoice's customer changes, the old edge must go. Who reconciles, and how does a connector express "this event's edges are the complete set for this subject"? Consider that events are append-only and a resync mints new event rows.

D5. Cardinality. An invoice belongs to exactly one customer. Enforce at write time, or detect after the fact? Note every existing edge type in this repo (member_of, about, mentions) is naturally many-to-many.

D6. Provenance. We want to be able to answer "which connector/rule asserted this edge" and "retract everything connector X asserted". There is a partial index on metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'relationshipTypeId' and ->>'ruleVersion' but it carries no org, connection, or rule name. events.id is a stored-version id that changes on resync, so it is NOT a stable provenance key. Owner interview 2026-08-16. **Read this before re-designing connector edges.**

## DECIDED by the owner
- **Schema is ORG-owned.** Connectors reference entity types and relationship
  types BY NAME and never create them. `lobu apply` already manages both
  (`packages/cli/src/commands/_lib/apply/client.ts`). This kills #2804 as a
  feature — it becomes "make the missing-type failure loud".
- **Manifest shape**: reference attributions by NAME, do not redeclare endpoints
  ([[reference_connector_edges_reuse_attributions_not_a_new_resolver]]).
- **ACL types**: deny first, grants later
  ([[reference_connector_declared_edges_acl_hole]]).
- **Milestone that matters: Prodma / ERP end to end.** Not breadth, not the
  general platform.
- **Who writes connectors**: first-party, PLUS customers authoring their own
  *with their coding agents*, plus eventually some public exposure. The realistic
  threat is therefore **an agent writing a plausible-but-wrong manifest**, not a
  malicious publisher. Publisher trust does not mitigate it.

## The org-owned-schema decision does NOT close the ACL hole
I claimed it did; that was wrong. **Lobu creates `member_of` itself** via
`ensureMemberOfType` on any Slack or GitHub ACL sync, so the type exists in an
org without anyone authoring it, and a connector can then reference it.

`entity_relationship_types` has **no owner/system column** — only a nullable
`created_by` that platform paths pass as `NULL`. It DOES have a `metadata` jsonb,
so stamping platform-owned types needs **no migration**.

## The actual code gap is ~40 lines + an SDK field
The connector sync path writes **ZERO** `entity_relationships` rows today, and
the manifest has **no** `relationships` field. Verified:
`git grep -c entity_relationships origin/main -- packages/server/src/utils/entity-link-upsert.ts packages/server/src/worker-api/run-lifecycle.ts packages/connectors/src` → no output.

But the hard part is already done: **`resolveLinksByKind`
(`entity-link-upsert.ts:734`) already tracks `byRule` and `matchesByRule` keyed
by rule AND item index**, inside `withEntityWriteTransaction`. So at the moment
both endpoints are resolved, the server is holding both entity ids in the same
transaction and simply drops them. What is missing:
1. `name?: string` on `EventAttributionRule`
2. `relationships?: [{ type, from, to }]` on the eventKind
3. a step reading it and calling `upsertEdges` with the two ids already in hand
4. resolve the type by slug; loud error if absent; refuse if platform-owned

## Still open (owner asked to be interviewed, artifact pending)
D1 manifest shape detail · D2 missing-type behavior (hard fail vs skip+surface)
· D3 how to protect ACL types · D4 **retraction** (invoice's customer changes —
who removes the old edge; events are append-only and resync mints new ids) ·
D5 cardinality (invoice→ONE customer; every existing type is many-to-many) ·
D6 provenance key.

## Also on the Prodma critical path
[[reference_entity_identities_collide_across_connections]] (#2798) — the identity
index excludes `connection_id`, so `erp_customer`/`CARI-001` in two tenants
collapses onto one entity. An ERP connector hits this immediately.

[[project_prodma_boundary_is_erp_of_record.md]]

/**

 * `force_delete_tree`'s hard delete stay where they are, because their SQL is
 * ordering-dependent and set-based.

import { type DbClient, getDb, pgBigintArray } from '../db/client';

interface EdgePair { fromEntityId: number; toEntityId: number; }

interface UpsertEdgesParams {
  db: DbClient;
  organizationId: string;
  relationshipTypeId: number;
  pairs: EdgePair[];
  source: string;
  confidence?: number | null;
  createdBy?: string | null;
  metadata?: object | null;
  onConflict: 'ignore' | 'update';

export async function ensureRelationshipType(params: {
  organizationId: string; slug: string; name: string; description: string;
}): Promise<number> { /* INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (organization_id, slug) WHERE status='active' DO UPDATE SET updated_at */ }

export async function upsertEdges(params: UpsertEdgesParams): Promise<number[]> {
  const { db, organizationId, relationshipTypeId, source, onConflict } = params;
  // `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` cannot affect the same row twice in one statement.
  // Self-edges are dropped rather than written: identity resolution can collapse
  // two source keys onto one entity, and a self-loop is meaningless for every
  // type written here.
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  const pairs: EdgePair[] = [];
  for (const pair of params.pairs) {
    if (pair.fromEntityId === pair.toEntityId) continue;
    const key = `${pair.fromEntityId}:${pair.toEntityId}`;
    if (seen.has(key)) continue;
    seen.add(key);
    pairs.push(pair);
  }
  if (pairs.length === 0) return [];
  const froms = pairs.map((p) => p.fromEntityId);
  const tos = pairs.map((p) => p.toEntityId);
  const conflictAction = onConflict === 'update'
    ? db`DO UPDATE SET metadata = EXCLUDED.metadata, source = EXCLUDED.source,
          updated_by = EXCLUDED.updated_by, updated_at = current_timestamp`
    : db`DO NOTHING`;
  const written = await db<{ id: number }>`
    INSERT INTO entity_relationships (
      organization_id, from_entity_id, to_entity_id, relationship_type_id,
      metadata, confidence, source, created_by, updated_by, created_at, updated_at
    )
    SELECT ${organizationId}, v.f, v.t, ${relationshipTypeId},
      ${params.metadata == null ? null : db.json(params.metadata)},
      ${params.confidence ?? null}, ${source},
      ${params.createdBy ?? null}, ${params.createdBy ?? null},
      current_timestamp, current_timestamp
    FROM unnest(${pgBigintArray(froms)}::bigint[], ${pgBigintArray(tos)}::bigint[]) AS v(f, t)
    ON CONFLICT (from_entity_id, to_entity_id, relationship_type_id)
      WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
    ${conflictAction}
    RETURNING id
  `;
  return written.map((row) => Number(row.id));
}

input.content:
Connector-declared edges · sign-off

Edge generation: what's left to decide

The connector sync path resolves both endpoint entities in the same transaction and then throws the pair away. Closing that is small. The six decisions below are what actually gate it — pick one option each and I'll build to the picks.

~60server lines, one new step in entity-link-upsert.ts
1SDK surface change — needs your sign-off per AGENTS.md
0new tables (D5 may add one column)
~150test lines

The batch writer this depends on (upsertEdges) is already built and green on the in-flight branch — 4 call sites consolidated, 7 contract tests, two mutations proved.

Why it's this small

resolveLinksByKind (entity-link-upsert.ts:734) already tracks byRule and matchesByRule keyed by rule and item index, inside withEntityWriteTransaction. At the moment an event's attributions resolve, the server is holding both entity ids in one transaction — it just has nowhere to put the relationship, because the manifest can't express one.

packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-types.ts   + name on EventAttributionRule, + relationships on eventKind
packages/server/src/utils/entity-link-upsert.ts + one step after resolveLinksByKind
packages/server/src/utils/edge-writes.ts        reused as-is (in flight)
packages/server/src/utils/…/relationship-types  + resolve-by-slug, no create

Everything expensive was already decided: the org owns the schema via lobu apply, so a connector references types by name and never mints them. That turns what looked like a schema-authoring feature into a lookup plus a failure mode.

D1

How does a connector name the two ends of an edge?

Forced by

EventAttributionRule[] is a positional array today — the rules have a role and a target, but nothing an edge could point at.

// Option A, on an ERP invoice kind
attributions: [
  { name: 'invoice',  role: 'about', target: { entityType: 'erp_invoice',  identities: [...] } },
  { name: 'customer', role: 'about', target: { entityType: 'erp_customer', identities: [...] } },
],
relationships: [
  { type: 'billed_to', from: 'invoice', to: 'customer' },
]
My takeA. It reuses the resolver that already works and adds exactly one concept. B is the version that quietly breaks — identities already collide across connections (#2798), so two independent resolutions of the same customer is a live bug, not a hypothetical.
Codexpending
D2

The manifest names a relationship type the org hasn't defined. Then what?

Forced by

You decided the org owns schema — so the connector can reference billed_to before anyone has run lobu apply to create it. Connectors will increasingly be written by customers' coding agents, so a plausible-but-wrong type name is the expected failure, not the rare one.

My takeB, and I want to be pedantic about what "surface" means. There is already a line in this exact file that logs a warning and returns null when an entity type is unknown — entity creates disappear and nobody finds out. If B is picked, the surfacing is part of the change, not a follow-up.
Codexpending
D3

What stops a connector from writing member_of?

Forced by

member_of is a live access gate. I previously said org-owned schema closed this hole — it doesn't: Lobu creates member_of itself via ensureMemberOfType on any Slack or GitHub ACL sync, so the type exists in orgs nobody authored it in. entity_relationship_types has no owner column — only a nullable created_by that platform paths pass as NULL.

My takeC. The friction argument against it mostly evaporates given your own decision — the org is already editing apply to create the type, so marking it writable in the same block costs one line. And it's the only option that's still correct for a gating type invented next quarter. A is the ship-today fallback if the apply surface is slower than you want.
Codexpending
D4

An invoice's customer changes upstream. Who removes the old edge?

Forced by

upsertEdges is additive. A resync mints a new event id for the same source item, so the corrected invoice arrives as a fresh event and writes invoice→customer_B while invoice→customer_A is still live. "Who is this invoice billed to" then has two answers — fatal for an ERP of record.

My takeB — and it's worth seeing that D4 and D5 are one decision wearing two hats. Cardinality is the only signal available at the moment a single event is processed. C is the option that looks cheapest and then leaks into every read path forever.
Codexpending
D5

Does a relationship type get a cardinality?

Forced by

Every relationship type today is effectively many-to-many; there's no cardinality anywhere. An invoice has exactly one bill-to customer. This is the one item on the page that changes a table — it needs an explicit yes from you.

My takeA. Cardinality is a genuine property of the relationship, not of the connector that happens to observe it, and it's the enforcement point D4 needs. B is the honest "not yet" — it works, it just doesn't hold anyone to it.
Codexpending
D6

What provenance does a connector-written edge carry?

Forced by

Disconnecting a connection has to be able to tombstone exactly the edges it created, and nothing else. relationship-validation.ts accepts only ui | llm | feed | api as caller-settable sources today.

My takeA, with connection_id mandatory rather than best-effort. The moment it's optional, the disconnect path has rows it can't classify and has to choose between leaving access behind and deleting someone else's edges.
Codexpending

What this doesn't cover

  • #2798, identity collision across connections — the identity index excludes connection_id, so erp_customer/CARI-001 in two tenants collapses onto one entity. An ERP connector hits this on day one, independently of every decision above.
  • Valid-time (#2801) — "billed to X as of March" isn't expressible; D4 gives correctness-now, not history.
  • Backfill — edges are written going forward. Existing events don't retroactively grow relationships without a migration pass.
D1 · D2 · D3 · D4 · D5 · D6 — nothing picked yet

1	My overall view: do not model this as “connectors create edges.” Model it as “connectors make versioned, retractable assertions; the server materializes the live edge graph.” Without that distinction, D4 and D6 cannot be made correct under multiple connectors.
2	
3	## D1 — Manifest shape
4	
5	**Recommendation: modified Option A / Option C.** Keep relationships separate from attributions, but use stable machine keys, not optional names.
6	
7	Add an additive `key?: string` to `EventAttributionRule`; require it whenever a relationship references that attribution. Add event-kind relationships shaped conceptually as: stable relationship `key`, relationship type slug, `from` attribution key, `to` attribution key, and explicit reconciliation mode.
8	
9	`name` is the wrong word. Everywhere else it implies a human-facing label that authors may freely rename. Provenance and retraction need an immutable identifier. The relationship itself also needs a stable key; endpoint names alone do not identify the rule across manifest versions.
10	
11	Option B is worse. Inline `relatesTo` makes one endpoint structurally privileged, makes reuse awkward, and still needs a forward reference. One attribution may participate in several edges, so relationships are naturally peer declarations over named resolved values.
12	
13	The strongest argument against separate relationships is verbosity: an AI author must name two attributions and then join them. That is real, but it buys deterministic validation and provenance. Good diagnostics can make the error actionable: duplicate key, unknown endpoint, missing type, or prohibited type.
14	
15	Failure modes:
16	
17	- The existing per-item return value loses rule identity—it is just `number[]`. Relationship resolution needs an `item index × attribution key → entity ID` result. The existing `byRule` and indexed entries make this a straightforward extension without re-resolving identities.
18	- Missing, null, ambiguous, and explicitly empty endpoints must not collapse into one state. An unresolved identity is an error; it must not be interpreted as “the complete desired edge set is empty.”
19	- Relationship-rule key removal or rename must retract the old rule’s assertions during connector-definition reconciliation. A rule version/hash is not a stable key.
20	- Validate relationship keys, attribution references, relationship types, endpoint type-pair rules, and protected types before a sync starts.
21	
22	The published SDK contract should remain additive: `key` can be optional for legacy attribution-only manifests, but conditionally mandatory when referenced by `relationships`.
23	
24	## D2 — Missing relationship type
25	
26	**Recommendation: Option A, plus the setup task from B.** Fail the run and surface an actionable setup notification. Do not skip the edge and advance the checkpoint.
27	
28	A relationship declaration is part of the connector’s declared output contract. Persisting the invoice event while silently omitting its customer edge creates a valid-looking but semantically incomplete workspace. For an incremental connector, the invoice may never be emitted again, so Option B creates a permanent hole unless you also build a durable event-reprojection mechanism.
29	
30	The best DX is to catch this before dispatch: connection/feed activation should enter `setup_required` with the exact missing type and expected endpoint types. Runtime lookup must still fail closed because schemas can drift after validation. A relationship-bound attribution whose entity type is missing should also become strict; keeping today’s warning/no-op there would merely move the silent failure one step earlier.
31	
32	The strongest argument against A is availability: an optional graph feature can stop useful raw ingestion. That is especially painful for public connectors installed into arbitrary organizations. The answer is preflight and setup UX, not corrupted partial output. If you later introduce an explicitly best-effort relationship mode backed by replayable stored events, that can opt into skipping. It should not be the default.
33	
34	Unconsidered failure: “fail the whole run” is not currently equivalent to transactional rollback. The real sync path commits streamed batches and events incrementally. A late failure can leave earlier batches committed. Preflight is therefore load-bearing; true whole-run atomicity would require staging/generation semantics. At runtime, at minimum, fail the current item/batch and never advance its checkpoint.
35	
36	## D3 — ACL-bearing relationship types
37	
38	**Recommendation: none of A–C is sufficient alone. Use B as the immediate safety gate, then introduce a first-class, non-user-settable authorization classification.**
39	
40	Immediately reject connector assertions for every relationship type consumed by authz, using one centralized registry shared by the ACL readers and connector writer. Do not rely on install consent. A connector that can mint `member_of` can mint authorization, and ordinary “read ERP data” consent is not an adequate privilege boundary.
41	
42	For the durable design, use a real `purpose = 'authorization'` or equivalent system-controlled classification—preferably a column, or protected metadata as an interim—and make both sides depend on it:
43	
44	- ACL queries only trust relationship types marked authorization-bearing.
45	- The connector assertion chokepoint categorically refuses those types.
46	
47	`metadata.owner='system'` alone is too broad and too easy to forget. System-created `mentions` is not equivalent to authorization. More importantly, if ACL reads continue trusting the slug alone, forgetting to stamp one future type produces a security hole. If the read itself requires the classification, forgetting the marker fails closed.
48	
49	The strongest argument against a hardcoded deny-list is drift and namespace capture. The repo already uses `member_of` as both a general domain term and an ACL primitive. Blocking it prevents legitimate domain modeling, while allowing it permits privilege escalation. Long term, ACL should use a reserved type such as `$acl_member_of`, or ideally a separate authorization graph.
50	
51	The particularly nasty existing failure is that `ensureMemberOfType` adopts any active org-local `member_of` row through `ON CONFLICT`, while authz checks only the slug. There is no reliable historical distinction between “platform-created” and “preexisting org type.” A migration must classify/adopt all current ACL incarnations deliberately; checking nullable `created_by` is not sufficient.
52	
53	Option C is a hard no. Consent is defense in depth, not the enforcement boundary for authorization writes.
54	
55	## D4 — Retraction
56	
57	**Recommendation: the server reconciles; the connector declares whether each relationship rule is authoritative.**
58	
59	Give each relationship rule an explicit mode such as `reconcile: 'replace'`. For each event item, that means: “for this stable source subject and this stable relationship rule, these resolved edges are the complete desired set.”
60	
61	The reconciliation scope should be based on stable source identity:
62	
63	`organization + connection + origin_id + relationship_rule_key`
64	
65	Include connector key for audit/filtering, but do not use `events.id`. A superseding event version has the same source subject and replaces the previous desired assertion set.
66	
67	The write flow should be:
68	
69	1. Resolve named attributions for the item.
70	2. Persist or find the current event version under the existing `(connection_id, origin_id)` serialization.
71	3. In that same `insertEvent` transaction/hook, upsert the desired assertions and deactivate this scope’s obsolete assertions.
72	4. Materialize or retract the live edge according to whether any active assertion still supports it.
73	
74	That shared event-write boundary is important: `afterPersist` runs for inserted, superseded, and unchanged events, so a manifest/rule change can reproject an unchanged source item. Writing edges earlier in the current attribution transaction could leave an edge committed when the later event insert fails.
75	
76	The strongest argument against server reconciliation is that the server cannot know whether a connector emitted a complete object or a partial patch. Correct—which is why `replace` must be explicit, not inferred. Append-only/inferred rules can use a different mode.
77	
78	Failure modes:
79	
80	- Distinguish an absent field from explicit `null`. For a `0..1` relationship, explicit null may mean clear; omitted data may mean partial payload and must not retract.
81	- For exactly-one, an unresolved or missing customer is an error, not an empty replacement set.
82	- A source deletion requires either a tombstone/update with the same `origin_id` and an empty desired set, or a separate full-feed snapshot protocol. Incremental silence cannot prove deletion.
83	- Never reconcile globally from one batch. Batches and pages are partial; reconcile only subjects actually observed.
84	- Rule removal, connector uninstall, and connection deletion need lifecycle-driven assertion retraction even if the source item never appears again.
85	
86	## D5 — Cardinality
87	
88	**Recommendation: enforce at write time. Detection afterward is monitoring, not correctness.**
89	
90	Cardinality belongs to the org-owned relationship-type schema, not the connector manifest. Otherwise two connectors can reference the same type while declaring incompatible semantics. Extend the relationship type’s allowed source/target rules with unambiguous constraints such as `minTargetsPerSource` and `maxTargetsPerSource`. Existing types default to unbounded many-to-many.
91	
92	For invoice → customer, `maxTargetsPerSource = 1`; if the domain truly requires a customer, `minTargetsPerSource = 1` is checked at the authoritative event boundary. Updating customer A to B must retract A and assert B atomically.
93	
94	The write kernel must serialize competing writes for the same source entity/type—via ordered entity locks or another Postgres-mediated lock—and every writer must pass through it. A post-insert query that discovers two customers has already exposed an invalid graph. The current live-triple index only prevents the exact same edge twice; it does not prevent invoice → customer A and invoice → customer B.
95	
96	The strongest argument against strict write-time enforcement is eventual consistency: partial ERP payloads, overlapping runs, or two producers may temporarily disagree. That is why minimum cardinality should apply only to explicitly authoritative snapshots. Maximum cardinality still must be enforced before making the conflicting edge live.
97	
98	Unconsidered failure: two independent producers can assert different customers for the same exact-one invoice. Do not silently choose the latest or overwrite the other producer. Reject/quarantine the conflicting assertion and surface it. Manual assertions participate in the same conflict; connector reconciliation must never erase them.
99	
100	## D6 — Provenance
101	
102	**Recommendation: add a normalized relationship-assertion ledger. Do not put one `derivedFrom` object on the edge and call it done.**
103	
104	The live edge and the assertion supporting it have different identity. Because the current unique index collapses all identical live triples, two connectors asserting the same edge cannot be represented as two `entity_relationships` rows. Conversely, storing only one producer in edge metadata means retracting connector X can incorrectly delete an edge still asserted by connector Y or a human.
105	
106	Each assertion needs two keys:
107	
108	The stable ownership/reconciliation scope:
109	
110	`organization_id, producer_kind, connector_key, connection_id, origin_id, relationship_rule_key`
111	
112	The claimed edge member:
113	
114	`relationship_type_id, from_entity_id, to_entity_id`
115	
116	Store `feed_key`, event kind, connector-definition version, manifest/rule version or hash, run ID, and the most recent stored event ID as audit evidence. They are not ownership identity. In particular, the stored event ID is useful for “which version most recently observed this?” but must never drive retraction.
117	
118	Index active assertions by exact reconciliation scope and separately by `(organization_id, connector_key, connection_id)` for bulk teardown. Then:
119	
120	- “Which connector/rule asserted this edge?” reads its active assertions.
121	- “Retract connection X” deactivates assertions by connection.
122	- “Retract every installation of connector X in this org” filters by org and connector key.
123	- The live edge is soft-deleted only when its last active assertion disappears.
124	
125	The existing JSON expression index on relationship type/rule version is inadequate: rule version is deliberately unstable, and it lacks connection, source subject, and rule identity. An array of assertions inside edge metadata looks cheaper but creates lost-update races, awkward indexing, and painful entity-merge handling.
126	
127	The strongest argument against an assertion table is complexity: another lifecycle, migration, materialization step, and entity-merge integration. But that complexity already exists in the domain. Keeping it implicit in mutable JSON does not remove it; it makes retraction nondeterministic.
128	
129	Additional failure modes include entity merges needing to repoint and coalesce assertions, relationship-type archive/recreation producing a new type incarnation, rule-key renames orphaning old scopes, and confidence/metadata conflicts between multiple producers.
130	
131	Bottom line: D1 modified A, D2 A with setup UX, D3 immediate deny-list plus a real ACL classification, D4 server-owned replace reconciliation, D5 write-time enforcement, and D6 a separate assertion ledger. I would not add direct connector inserts into `entity_relationships` before the assertion/reconciliation boundary exists.
132	
133	No files were modified.

Codex's thesis, and the three claims I checked

Its position is that D4 and D6 cannot be made correct under multiple producers without that split, and that it would not ship direct connector inserts into entity_relationships before the assertion boundary exists.

---
name: reference_connector_edges_must_write_from_afterpersist_not_attributions
description: "Connector edges CANNOT be written from the attribution transaction — it commits before any event row exists. Write from insertEvent's afterPersist hook instead. Verified in run-lifecycle.ts."
metadata:
  type: reference
---

I sized connector edge generation at "~60 lines, one step after `resolveLinksByKind`".
**That seam is wrong.** codex caught it; the code says so outright.

`run-lifecycle.ts:292-296`, verbatim:
> The real path passes the singleton: **event inserts below remain
> statement-per-autocommit, while `applyEventAttributions` opens one bounded
> transaction** for this batch's entity attribution writes.

So `applyEventAttributions` runs **before** the event inserts, in **its own
transaction**. Writing edges there commits an edge that no event supports, and a
failing event insert cannot retract it.

## Consequences (all verified, not inferred)
- **"Fail the run" is not a rollback.** Events autocommit per statement, so a late
  failure leaves earlier batches committed. Any fail-closed policy must fail the
  *item* and refuse to advance its checkpoint — and the real fix is preflight at
  connection activation, before dispatch.
- **The correct seam is `afterPersist`** (`insert-event.ts:388` signature).
  It receives `(event, sql)` inside the insert's transaction.
- **`afterPersist` fires for `unchanged` events too** — `insert-event.ts:440` for
  the unchanged path, `:630` for persisted. That is what makes rule-keyed
  reprojection possible: a manifest change can re-derive edges for a source item
  that did not change.
- Passing a caller `sql` makes `insertEvent` **skip its advisory-lock dedup
  transaction** (the caller's tx is assumed to be the atomic scope). That lock is
  what serializes concurrent ingests of the same `(connection_id, origin_id)`
  across replicas — do not casually take it over.

## Reconciliation scope
Key on `organization + connection_id + origin_id + relationship_rule_key`.
**Never `events.id`** — a superseding version is the same source subject
([[reference_events_metadata_watcher_id_means_about_not_produced]] neighbours this;
the `events.id`-is-a-version fact is in AGENTS.md).

---
name: reference_ensure_member_of_type_adopts_any_existing_org_type
description: "ensureMemberOfType ON CONFLICT ADOPTS a pre-existing org-created member_of type — so an org's own domain type gets silently promoted into the ACL path. No way to tell platform from org origin."
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`ensureMemberOfType` (`packages/server/src/authz/access-graph.ts`) is:

```sql
INSERT INTO entity_relationship_types (slug, name, ..., created_by, ...)
VALUES ('member_of', 'Member of', ..., NULL, ...)
ON CONFLICT (organization_id, slug) WHERE status = 'active'
DO UPDATE SET updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
RETURNING id
```

It does **not** create-or-fail. It **adopts**: if the org already has an active
`member_of` row — created by `lobu apply` for ordinary domain modelling — this
returns *that* row's id and Lobu starts writing ACL edges onto the org's own type.

**There is no historical distinction between platform-created and org-created.**
`created_by` is `NULL` on the platform path, and nullable everywhere else. Any
migration that classifies ACL types must deliberately adopt every current
incarnation; checking `created_by` proves nothing.

## Why this matters for the edge design
It kills two tempting D3 answers:
- A deny-list on the slug `member_of` blocks legitimate domain modelling AND is a
  text matcher on a security boundary ([[feedback_text_matcher_is_never_the_boundary]]).
- "Only the org can author the type, so org-owned schema closes the hole" is
  false — I asserted this and it was wrong.

codex's answer, which I agree with: a system-controlled `purpose='authorization'`
classification that **the ACL reads depend on**, not just the writer. Then
forgetting to classify a new gating type fails closed instead of opening a hole.
Long-term it wants ACL on a reserved slug (`$acl_member_of`) so the namespace
stops being shared with domain vocabulary.

Related: [[reference_connector_declared_edges_acl_hole]] ·
[[project_connector_declared_edges_decision_state]]

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
refactor(server): consolidate hand-rolled edge upserts into one batch writer

Four materializers had each hand-rolled the same INSERT into
entity_relationships, one round trip per edge. Three agreed on the
statement; auto-linker had copied it WITHOUT the ON CONFLICT clause and
put a SELECT in front instead, so two concurrent linkers could both pass
the check and the second raise 23505 against the live-triple index.

upsertEdges takes the whole batch in one statement, targets the partial
live-triple index, and dedupes within the batch — ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
refuses to affect a row twice, so an un-deduped batch raises 21000.
Self-edges are dropped rather than written: identity resolution can
collapse two source keys onto one entity and a self-loop is meaningless
for every type written here.

Not a replacement for relationship-validation.ts, which guards the
caller-facing manage_entity surface — its validateSource accepts only
ui|llm|feed|api and would reject the config/manual sources reconcilers
own, and checkDuplicateEdge raises a 409 where a materializer wants an
idempotent no-op. entity-merge's repoint/tombstone and force_delete_tree's
hard delete stay put; their SQL is ordering-dependent and set-based.

Both failure modes are covered by mutation-proved tests: removing the
conflict clause reproduces the 23505, removing the in-batch dedupe
reproduces the 21000.
EOF

## Summary
- Four materializers (`access-graph`, `channel-about`, `github-team-graph`, `auto-linker`) had each hand-rolled the same `INSERT INTO entity_relationships`, one round trip per edge. `upsertEdges` writes the whole batch in one statement.
- **This fixes a real bug.** Three of the four agreed on the statement; `auto-linker` had copied it *without* the `ON CONFLICT` clause and put a `SELECT` in front instead, so two concurrent linkers could both pass the check and the second raise `23505` against `idx_entity_relationships_live_triple`.
- Net −38 lines across the call sites; `github-team-graph`'s duplicate local `ensureMemberOfType` is deleted in favour of the one in `access-graph`.

## Scope — what this deliberately does not touch
Not a replacement for `relationship-validation.ts`, which guards the caller-facing `manage_entity` surface: its `validateSource` accepts only `ui|llm|feed|api` and would reject the `config`/`manual` sources these reconcilers own, and `checkDuplicateEdge` raises a 409 where a materializer wants an idempotent no-op.

Not a general edge kernel either — `entity-merge`'s repoint/tombstone and `force_delete_tree`'s hard delete stay where they are, because their SQL is ordering-dependent and set-based.

## Test plan
- [x] Intended files staged explicitly, then `make pre-pr-remote` clean (Depot run `v7jg6h0sf2`, zero failed jobs, full remote preflight recorded for tree `59fc7fd8`)
- [x] Tests run: `bunx vitest run` in `packages/server` — 448/448 green on the full sweep; 7 new contract tests in `edge-writes-batch.test.ts`
- [x] Bug fix: red→fix→green below

### red → green
Both failure modes were mutation-proved rather than asserted.

Removing the `ON CONFLICT` clause (the `auto-linker` bug, reproduced):

```
duplicate key value violates unique constraint "idx_entity_relationships_live_triple"
  × survives two concurrent writers claiming the same pair
```

Removing the in-batch dedupe:

```
ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
  × dedupes within one batch so DO UPDATE cannot hit a row twice
```

With both in place: `7 passed (7)`.

## Notes
The tombstone test pins behaviour worth stating explicitly: the conflict target is the **partial** live-triple index, so a soft-deleted row is not a conflict and cannot be revived by the update branch — a re-assertion writes a fresh live row beside the tombstone.

Self-edges are dropped rather than written. Identity resolution can collapse two source keys onto one entity (see #2798), and a self-loop is meaningless for every relationship type written on these paths.

content.text:
Sized it against the code. Short answer: **~1,300 lines across three PRs to get Prodma working, plus a fourth PR (~700) you don't need until a second producer exists.** That's bigger than my "~60 lines" but much smaller than codex's framing implies, and while measuring I found the thing that resolves your simple-vs-reliable tension for free.

## The free reliability win

`insertEvent` already opens an **advisory-lock transaction keyed on `(connection_id, origin_id)`** that serializes concurrent ingests of the same source item across replicas. The comment in `run-lifecycle.ts` spells it out — passing a caller-supplied `sql` is what makes it *skip* that lock.

So if edges are written from `afterPersist` **without** passing a caller handle, same-subject edge writes are serialized across replicas at no cost. That kills the piece I was most worried about: codex says max-cardinality enforcement needs ordered entity locks or another Postgres-mediated lock, and it's right in general — but not for phase 1, because the reconciliation scope *is* `(connection_id, origin_id)` and that lock already exists. **No new locking primitive, no deadlock surface.** Cross-producer conflict is a ledger-phase problem, which is exactly where D7=B puts it.

## The estimate

| | scope | lines | confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PR A** | ACL `purpose` classification (D3) | ~250 | **75** |
| **PR B** | SDK surface + preflight validation (D1, D2) | ~390 | **80** |
| **PR C** | Edge write from `afterPersist` + cardinality (D4, D5, D7) | ~630 | **70** |
| **PR D** | Assertion ledger (D6) — deferred | ~700 | **35** |

**PR A is smaller than I feared and should ship first, separately.** The ACL read surface is exactly three sites, all doing `rt.slug = 'member_of'` (`channel-visibility.ts:190`, `resource-visibility.ts:103`, `channel-messages-visibility.ts:118`). Adding `AND rt.purpose = 'authorization'` is six lines. It's independent of connector edges and fixes something live today — an org that defines `member_of` in their own apply schema gets it adopted into the ACL path right now.

**PR C is smaller than codex's framing suggests**, because `resolveEventAttributionsForItems` (the webhook path) *already* returns resolved entity ids keyed by item index. `applyEventAttributions` runs the same core resolver and just declares `Promise<void>` — it throws the answer away. Phase 1 is largely "return what the sibling function already returns, thread it to the insert loop."

**Confidence 35 on PR D is the honest number** and the reason I'd hold it. New table, lifecycle, materialization, entity-merge integration, teardown paths — I haven't decomposed it, and 700 is a guess, not an estimate.

## What I'd cut

Nothing from A–C, but I'd narrow D5: enforce max-cardinality **within the reconciliation scope only**, where the advisory lock already makes it correct. Skip cross-producer conflict quarantine until the ledger. That's codex's correctness argument honored where it's reachable and deferred where it isn't — single producer per scope is enforced by construction in phase 1, not assumed.

## One thing I'm not confident about

PR A's migration has a decision I can't make from the code. When `ensureMemberOfType` finds an existing unclassified `member_of`, adopting-and-stamping it preserves today's behavior but permanently blesses whatever the org created. Refusing it breaks ACL for those orgs. Codex's cleaner answer — move ACL to a reserved slug like `$acl_member_of` — avoids the collision entirely but turns PR A into a data migration of existing ACL edges, which roughly doubles it and makes it genuinely risky. I'd want to query prod for how many orgs have a `member_of` type that Lobu didn't create before choosing. That's a read-only query I can run.

**Overall confidence: 70.** Basis: the three structural facts driving the sizing are read from `origin/main` source, not inferred — the advisory lock, the three ACL read sites, and the webhook resolver's existing return shape. What I haven't done is write any of it, and PR D is unmeasured.

**Next actions:**
1. Run the prod read-only query on unexplained `member_of` types — it decides PR A's shape before I write it.
2. Start PR A once that answers; it's independent and unblocks everything.
3. `make review` on #2824 is still running — I'll report the verdict.
4. Decompose PR D properly before you commit to the ledger; 35 confidence isn't a number to plan against.

input.content:
You reviewed a connector-declared-edge design earlier and raised: (a) model connectors as making versioned retractable assertions, not writing edges; (b) write from insertEvent's afterPersist, not the attribution transaction; (c) an ACL `purpose` classification that READS depend on; (d) a separate assertion ledger.

The owner has now signed off on a plan. Your job is ONLY to find GAPS — things that will bite us that this plan does not address, or places where the plan is internally inconsistent. Do not re-argue decisions already made. Be concrete and cite mechanisms, not principles. If you think a phase is mis-ordered or a phase boundary leaks, say exactly how.

Repo: Lobu (Bun monorepo, packages/server, packages/connector-sdk, Postgres). Read the code before asserting.

## Settled decisions
- D1: attributions get an immutable `key`; eventKind gets `relationships: [{type, from, to}]` referencing those keys; relationship rules get their own stable key.
- D2: fail closed. Preflight at connection activation (`setup_required`) naming the missing relationship type; runtime also fails the item and does NOT advance its checkpoint.
- D3: system-controlled `purpose='authorization'` classification. ACL READS require it; the connector write path categorically refuses those types.
- D4: reconciliation scope = organization + connection_id + origin_id + relationship_rule_key. Never events.id. `reconcile:'replace'` declared per rule. Omitted field != explicit null.
- D5: cardinality on the relationship TYPE (org-owned schema), enforced at write.
- D6: assertion ledger — DEFERRED to phase 4.
- D7: phase 1-3 ship single-producer; the ledger lands before a second producer exists.

## Phasing
- PR A (~250 lines): add `purpose` column; classify existing rows; 3 ACL read sites (channel-visibility.ts:190, resource-visibility.ts:103, channel-messages-visibility.ts:118) gain `AND rt.purpose='authorization'`; ensureMemberOfType stamps on create.
- PR B (~390): SDK `key` + `relationships`; publish/activation-time validation.
- PR C (~630): applyEventAttributions returns per-item resolved ids (mirroring what resolveEventAttributionsForItems already returns); edges written from afterPersist; reconciliation by the D4 scope; cardinality enforced.
