4/4. Now the thing I won't merge past without you.

**The version-skew window is worse than the review thought.** It assumed `Recreate` (one live version at a time). Prod actually runs **`RollingUpdate` with 2 replicas** — I checked the live deployment, and the chart default is overridden. So old and new pods serve *simultaneously* during a rollout.

The consequence: the migration swaps the unique index, and every already-running pod still issues the 3-column `ON CONFLICT`, which no longer matches any index. Those writes fail with *"there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification"* for the whole rollout, not a brief hook window. That hits identity inserts on connector sync, chat/Slack claims, sign-in member claims, canvas events, and automation entity promotion. Syncs retry; sign-in claims surface to the user.

Worse, it's not symmetric: **rolling the image back after the migration breaks identity writes until you roll forward again.**

This is the same shape as the ACL trigger lesson already in my notes — ship inert, arm later. The clean fix is two releases: this PR creates the new index *alongside* the old one so both pod versions resolve, and a follow-up drops the old index once the rollout has drained. The cost is that connection scoping stays inert until PR 2 (which is free — no connector declares `scope` yet, and the reviewer confirmed that), and my collision test has to move to PR 2 with it.

Not merging on my own judgment, because the two options differ in a way only you should pick:

options.label: Two releases — ship inert, arm after rollout (Recommended)
options.description: This PR adds the column and creates the new 4-col index ALONGSIDE the old one, so old pods (3-col) and new pods (4-col) both resolve. No skew window, rollback stays safe. Connection scoping is inert until a follow-up PR drops the old index — which costs nothing today since no connector declares `scope` yet. Same ship-inert-then-arm pattern as the ACL trigger. Cost: my collision test moves to PR 2, plus one extra PR cycle.

options.label: Merge as-is, accept the window
options.description: Single PR, done tonight. Identity writes error from old pods for the ~30-90s rollout, and an image rollback breaks them until you roll forward. Nothing corrupts — it's failed writes, and syncs retry — but sign-in member claims and chat identity claims are user-visible. Defensible given the table is tiny and traffic is low, but it is a real (small) incident.

options.label: Merge as-is but drain first
options.description: Same single PR, but you scale the app to 0 replicas before the migration and back up after, turning RollingUpdate into a manual Recreate. Removes the skew window at the cost of a brief full outage instead of degraded writes. Rollback exposure remains.

input.command:
gh pr comment 2846 --body "**Accepted risk: rollout version skew.** Landing this knowingly, recorded so it is not a surprise.

Swapping \`idx_entity_identities_live_unique\` to the 4-column form means an already-running pod's 3-column \`ON CONFLICT\` no longer matches any index, and those identity inserts fail with *\"there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification\"*.

The review noted this but assumed it was bounded by \`app.strategy: Recreate\` (one live version). That is the chart default (\`charts/lobu/values.yaml:30\`) but **prod overrides it** — the live deployment is \`RollingUpdate\` with 2 replicas:

\`\`\`
\$ kubectl -n summaries-prod get deploy summaries-app-lobu-app -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}'
RollingUpdate
\`\`\`

So old and new pods serve simultaneously for the rollout (~30-90s), and identity inserts from old pods fail during it. Affected paths: connector sync attribution, chat/Slack identity claims, sign-in member claims, canvas events, automation entity promotion. Syncs retry; sign-in claims are user-visible.

Also asymmetric: **rolling the image back after this migration breaks identity writes until you roll forward again.**

Nothing corrupts — these are failed writes, not bad data. The alternative was two releases (create the new index alongside the old, drop the old once the rollout drains, same ship-inert-then-arm pattern as the ACL trigger), which was weighed and declined in favour of landing now. Worth revisiting if this class of migration recurs on a busier table; \`entity_identities\` is 9,815 rows / 4 MB today.

Reviewer disclosure: \`pi-review\` was produced by \`REVIEWER_CLI=claude CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL=opus\` — same model family as the author. Both independent pools were exhausted (codex/\`pi\`: \`usage limit ... try again at Aug 20th\`; Fable 5: its own limit). Same as #2843/#2844." 2>&1 | tail -1

input.command:
cd /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu && gh issue create --title "Identity scope is declared per usage, not per namespace — conflicting declarations silently fork an entity" --body "Follow-up to #2798 / #2846, which added \`EntityIdentitySpec.scope\`.

## What

\`scope\` sits on \`EntityIdentitySpec\`, which lives inside each \`attributions[].target.identities[]\` entry. A connector that references the same namespace from two event kinds can therefore declare two different scopes for it, and nothing validates the pair.

\`\`\`ts
// feeds.customers.eventKinds.customer
identities: [{ namespace: 'erp_customer', eventPath: '...', scope: 'connection' }]

// feeds.invoices.eventKinds.invoice  — same namespace, no scope
identities: [{ namespace: 'erp_customer', eventPath: '...' }]
\`\`\`

## Why it matters

The two write different rows for the same value — one with \`scope_connection_id = <conn>\`, one with NULL — and the live-unique index treats them as distinct. The result is **two entities for one real customer**, created silently, with traits and events split across them. No error, no warning; it looks like a data-quality problem rather than a manifest bug.

Scope is a property of what the namespace *means* in the source system, so two usages disagreeing is always an authoring mistake, never a legitimate configuration.

## Options

1. **Preflight validation** — reject a connector definition whose namespace carries more than one distinct \`scope\` across all its feeds/event kinds. Cheap, catches it at declaration time, and preflight is where the other manifest contradictions are already caught.
2. **Move the declaration up** — put scope on the namespace rather than the usage (\`ConnectorIdentityModule\` / the namespace registry), making the conflict unrepresentable. Cleaner but a larger surface change, and connector-authored namespaces are not in the core registry today.

(1) looks right as the immediate fix; (2) is the shape to converge on if identity declarations get consolidated later.

## Not urgent

No connector declares \`scope\` yet, so this is currently unreachable. It becomes reachable with the first connection-scoped connector, which is the ERP work." 2>&1 | tail -1

input.command:
gh issue create --title "Changing a namespace's identity scope after rows exist forks every entity — no backfill or detection" --body "Follow-up to #2798 / #2846.

## What

\`scope\` is applied at write time and baked into \`entity_identities.scope_connection_id\`. There is no path for changing it once rows exist.

Ship a connector with \`erp_customer\` unscoped, sync, then correct it to \`scope: 'connection'\`:

- existing rows keep \`scope_connection_id IS NULL\`
- the next sync writes \`scope_connection_id = <conn>\`
- the two never match, so **every customer is re-minted as a new entity**

The reverse direction (connection → organization) is worse: the new org-scoped write can collide with a *different* connection's row for the same identifier, merging two tenants' records.

## Why it matters

Getting scope right on the first try requires knowing whether a third-party namespace is globally unique before you have any data from it. Correcting it is the expected path, not an edge case — and today that correction silently doubles the entity count instead of erroring.

## What is missing

1. **Detection** — nothing notices that a manifest's declared scope disagrees with the scope of rows already stored for that namespace. A preflight comparison against \`entity_identities\` would catch it at declare time.
2. **Migration** — no supported way to re-scope existing rows. Organization→connection is mechanical when exactly one connection wrote them (\`scope_connection_id = connection_id\`, which is already recorded as provenance); it is ambiguous when several did, and that ambiguity is the real reason the namespace was mis-declared.
3. **Guidance** — the SDK doc comment explains what scope means but says nothing about it being effectively immutable once synced.

At minimum this should fail loudly instead of forking. Related: #2847 (the same absence of validation, in the conflicting-declaration direction)." 2>&1 | tail -1

result.output: https://github.com/lobu-ai/lobu/issues/2848

input.command:
gh issue create --title "Reconnecting a connection re-mints every connection-scoped entity (scope keys on connections.id)" --body "Follow-up to #2798 / #2846. **The most likely of the three to produce bad production data**, because the trigger is a routine operation rather than an authoring mistake.

## What

\`entity_identities.scope_connection_id\` stores \`connections.id\`. That column is a bigserial and is never reused, so deleting a connection and re-creating it — reconnect, re-auth that recreates the row, delete-and-re-add to fix a setting — yields a different id.

Consequences for a connection-scoped namespace:

- every existing identity row stays pinned to the **old** id and can never match again
- the new connection matches nothing and **re-mints the entire entity set**
- the old entities remain, still carrying their events and traits

For an ERP connection that is the whole customer list duplicated, with history split across the two copies.

## Why the FK decision does not cover this

#2846 deliberately gave the column no foreign key, and that reasoning stands: \`ON DELETE SET NULL\` would silently promote a connection-scoped identity to org-wide (the exact collapse the column prevents), and \`CASCADE\` would delete identity rows and take their entities' attribution with them.

The migration comment describes the dangling id as \"inert\". That is true of the row and false of the outcome — the row is inert precisely *because* nothing matches it, which is what forces the re-mint.

## Options

1. **Key scope on something stabler than the row id.** A per-connection external identity — the provider account/tenant/workspace id the connection authenticates as — survives reconnection, which is exactly the property wanted. It is also the more honest model: two connections to the *same* ERP tenant arguably should share identities, and today they would not.
2. **Re-scope on connection replacement.** Detect that a new connection targets the same external account and repoint existing \`scope_connection_id\` rows to it. Keeps the current column, needs a reliable notion of \"same account\" — i.e. option 1's key anyway.
3. **Accept and document**, with an operator-facing warning at delete time that reconnecting will duplicate entities for connection-scoped namespaces.

(1) is the real fix and subsumes (2).

## Reachability

Currently unreachable — no connector declares \`scope\`. It becomes reachable with the first connection-scoped connector, so this should be decided **before** the ERP connector work (#2812 / connector-declared edges) rather than after." 2>&1 | tail -1

1. Merge #2846 when the gate and re-review land, then prod-verify the migration applied and the index is the 4-column form.
2. Watch the rollout — that's when the accepted skew window is live. If identity-write errors spike, roll *forward*, not back.
3. Decide #2849 before any connection-scoped connector ships; it's the one that makes bad data rather than a bad test.

=== reference pattern ===
-- migrate:up transaction:false

-- Arbiter for org-scoped artifact rows: one row per (org, key, version).
-- Built before the shared arbiter and before the old global unique is retired
-- (20260721120040) so writes are never left without uniqueness.
--
-- The INVALID-carcass heal is inlined here (not a standalone companion
-- migration) so it re-runs on every retry. A separate heal migration records
-- as applied on its first success; if THIS CONCURRENTLY build then crashes it
-- leaves an INVALID same-named carcass, and the retry — which skips the
-- already-applied heal — never clears it, so CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS silently
-- no-ops over the carcass and records this migration as applied with a
-- non-enforcing INVALID index (a silent cross-org uniqueness hole). Inlined,
-- the heal drops the carcass on every attempt so the build always converges.
-- The runners split transaction:false sections statement-at-a-time (prod:
-- scripts/migrate-up.mjs; embedded/tests: db/migration-loader.ts), so the heal
-- DO and the CONCURRENTLY build each run unwrapped — CONCURRENTLY is never
-- trapped in an implicit multi-statement transaction.
DO $heal$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM pg_index i
    JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
    JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
    WHERE n.nspname = 'public'
      AND c.relname = 'connector_versions_org_key_version'
      AND NOT i.indisvalid
  ) THEN
    EXECUTE 'DROP INDEX public.connector_versions_org_key_version';
  END IF;
END
$heal$;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS connector_versions_org_key_version
  ON public.connector_versions (organization_id, connector_key, version)
  WHERE organization_id IS NOT NULL;

-- migrate:down transaction:false

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.connector_versions_org_key_version;

content.text: Following the repo's established pattern (`transaction:false` + INVALID-carcass heal + `CONCURRENTLY`), with a new index name since the same name can't be built while the old exists:

input.content:
-- migrate:up transaction:false

-- Identity scope: does an identifier mean the same thing across connections?
--
-- `idx_entity_identities_live_unique` is `(organization_id, namespace,
-- identifier)`, so two connections in the same org that share a namespace
-- collapse onto one entity. Namespaces come from connector manifests, not from
-- anything the platform controls: two ERP connections against two different
-- tenants both declaring `erp_customer` resolve `CARI-001` in tenant A to the
-- entity minted for `CARI-001` in tenant B. Nothing errors — the second
-- connection's attribution silently accretes traits onto the first's entity.
--
-- The fix is NOT to add `connection_id` to the index. That column is
-- PROVENANCE: it records which connection first wrote the row, and it is set on
-- every connector-written identity including ones that are legitimately
-- org-wide. Indexing it would split identities that must stay collapsed — in
-- production today one organization shares `slack_channel_id` across three
-- connections and `slack_user_id` across two, and the same Slack user seen
-- through two connections must remain ONE person.
--
-- So scope gets its own column, written only when the connector declares the
-- namespace connection-scoped. NULL means org-wide, which is every row that
-- exists today.
--
-- Deliberately NO foreign key, unlike the sibling `connection_id`
-- (`entity_identities_connection_id_fkey`, ON DELETE SET NULL). That column is
-- provenance, so nulling it on a deleted connection loses nothing. This one is
-- part of the uniqueness key: SET NULL would silently PROMOTE a
-- connection-scoped identity to org-wide — the exact collapse the column
-- prevents — and could collide with a legitimately org-wide row for the same
-- (org, namespace, identifier), aborting the connection delete on a unique
-- violation. CASCADE would delete identity rows, taking their entities'
-- attribution with them. The dangling id is inert for matching; the entity
-- duplication that follows a reconnect is tracked separately (#2849).
--
-- Nullable with no default, so this is a metadata-only catalog update: no table
-- rewrite and no lingering ACCESS EXCLUSIVE hold.
ALTER TABLE entity_identities
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS scope_connection_id bigint;

-- The replacement arbiter is built CONCURRENTLY under a NEW name and the old
-- one retired afterwards, so uniqueness is never absent and neither statement
-- takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the duration of a build. The same name cannot be
-- reused while the old index still exists, and that is fine: `ON CONFLICT`
-- infers its arbiter by matching the target EXPRESSION against available
-- indexes, never by name.
--
-- COALESCE to a sentinel rather than indexing the nullable column directly: in
-- a UNIQUE index NULLs are distinct, so a bare `scope_connection_id` would stop
-- deduplicating the org-wide rows entirely — every re-sync would insert another
-- copy. 0 is safe as the sentinel because `connections.id` is a bigserial and
-- never 0.
--
-- Existing rows all have NULL, so they collapse on exactly the key they
-- collapse on today: this migration is behaviour-preserving on its own, and
-- only a connector declaring `scope: 'connection'` changes any outcome.
--
-- The INVALID-carcass heal is inlined rather than split into its own migration
-- so it re-runs on every retry: a crashed CONCURRENTLY build leaves an INVALID
-- same-named index, and `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` would then silently no-op
-- over it and record this migration as applied with a NON-ENFORCING arbiter —
-- a silent uniqueness hole on identity claims. Same structure as
-- 20260721120020_connector_versions_org_unique.sql.
DO $heal$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM pg_index i
    JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
    JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
    WHERE n.nspname = 'public'
      AND c.relname = 'idx_entity_identities_live_unique_scoped'
      AND NOT i.indisvalid
  ) THEN
    EXECUTE 'DROP INDEX public.idx_entity_identities_live_unique_scoped';
  END IF;
END
$heal$;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_entity_identities_live_unique_scoped
  ON public.entity_identities (organization_id, namespace, identifier, COALESCE(scope_connection_id, 0))
  WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.idx_entity_identities_live_unique;

-- migrate:down transaction:false

-- Reversible only while no connection-scoped identities exist. Once two
-- connections hold the same (org, namespace, identifier) under different
-- scopes, rebuilding the narrower arbiter makes them duplicates and the CREATE
-- fails — which is the correct failure: silently collapsing two different
-- tenants' customers onto one entity is the defect this column exists to
-- prevent, and the rollback must not perform it. A failed CONCURRENTLY build
-- leaves an INVALID carcass, healed on the next attempt by the block above.
DO $heal_down$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM pg_index i
    JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indexrelid
    JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
    WHERE n.nspname = 'public'
      AND c.relname = 'idx_entity_identities_live_unique'
      AND NOT i.indisvalid
  ) THEN
    EXECUTE 'DROP INDEX public.idx_entity_identities_live_unique';
  END IF;
END
$heal_down$;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_entity_identities_live_unique
  ON public.entity_identities (organization_id, namespace, identifier)
  WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.idx_entity_identities_live_unique_scoped;

ALTER TABLE entity_identities
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS scope_connection_id;

#!/bin/sh
set -eu

kubectl_bin=${KUBECTL_BIN:-/migration-tools/kubectl}
namespace=${NAMESPACE:?NAMESPACE is required}
app_deployment=${APP_DEPLOYMENT:?APP_DEPLOYMENT is required}
app_selector=${APP_SELECTOR:?APP_SELECTOR is required}
worker_deployment=${WORKER_DEPLOYMENT:-}
worker_selector=${WORKER_SELECTOR:-}
timeout=${QUIESCE_TIMEOUT:-300s}
pending_check=${MIGRATION_PENDING_CHECK:-}
quiescence_started=0
app_replicas=absent
worker_replicas=absent

deployment_replicas() {
  deployment=$1
  replicas=$("$kubectl_bin" --namespace "$namespace" get deployment "$deployment" \
    --ignore-not-found --output 'jsonpath={.spec.replicas}')
  if [ -z "$replicas" ]; then
    printf 'absent'
    return
  fi
  printf '%s' "$replicas"
}

restore_deployment() {
  deployment=$1
  replicas=$2
  if [ "$replicas" = absent ]; then
    return
  fi
  echo "restoring deployment $deployment to $replicas replicas"
  "$kubectl_bin" --namespace "$namespace" scale deployment "$deployment" \
    --replicas="$replicas"
}

restore_on_failure() {
  status=$?
  trap - EXIT INT TERM
  if [ "$status" -ne 0 ] && [ "$quiescence_started" -eq 1 ]; then
    echo "migration failed with status $status; restoring old deployments" >&2
    restore_failed=0
    restore_deployment "$app_deployment" "$app_replicas" || restore_failed=1
    if [ -n "$worker_deployment" ]; then
      restore_deployment "$worker_deployment" "$worker_replicas" || restore_failed=1
    fi
    if [ "$restore_failed" -ne 0 ]; then
      echo "ERROR: migration failed and one or more deployments could not be restored" >&2
    fi
  fi
  exit "$status"
}

# Quiescing scales the app to zero for the length of a pod restart, which the
# ingress answers with 503. Only a schema change needs that window, and most
# deploys ship none, so ask the ledger first. Fail closed: only the check's
# definitive "nothing pending" status (3) skips the quiesce -- an unset check
# or any other status, including a crash, still quiesces.
migrations_pending() {
  if [ -z "$pending_check" ]; then
    echo 'no pending-migration check configured; quiescing'
    return 0
  fi
  set +e
  # Word splitting is intended: the check is configured as a full command line.
  $pending_check
  pending_status=$?
  set -e
  # 3 is CHECK_PENDING_NONE_EXIT in scripts/migrate-up.mjs -- the one status
  # that means "the ledger was read and it is complete".
  if [ "$pending_status" -eq 3 ]; then
    return 1
  fi
  if [ "$pending_status" -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "pending-migration check failed with status $pending_status; quiescing" >&2
  fi
  return 0
}

quiesce_deployment() {
  deployment=$1
  selector=$2
  replicas=$3
  if [ "$replicas" = absent ]; then
    echo "deployment $deployment is absent; nothing to quiesce"
    return
  fi
  "$kubectl_bin" --namespace "$namespace" scale deployment "$deployment" --replicas=0
  pods=$("$kubectl_bin" --namespace "$namespace" get pods \
    --selector "$selector" --output name)
  if [ -n "$pods" ]; then
    "$kubectl_bin" --namespace "$namespace" wait --for=delete pod \
      --selector "$selector" --timeout "$timeout"
  fi
}

if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo 'migration command is required' >&2
  exit 2
fi

trap restore_on_failure EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT
trap 'exit 143' TERM

if migrations_pending; then
  app_replicas=$(deployment_replicas "$app_deployment")
  if [ -n "$worker_deployment" ]; then
    worker_replicas=$(deployment_replicas "$worker_deployment")
  fi

  quiescence_started=1
  quiesce_deployment "$app_deployment" "$app_selector" "$app_replicas"
  if [ -n "$worker_deployment" ]; then
    quiesce_deployment "$worker_deployment" "$worker_selector" "$worker_replicas"
  fi
  echo 'all old database clients are quiesced; running migration'
else
  echo 'no pending migrations; skipping quiesce so Helm can roll without downtime'
fi

"$@"
echo 'migration completed; Helm may apply the new deployments'

---
name: reference-migrations-quiesce-the-app-to-zero-so-there-is-no-version-skew
description: A pending migration scales app+worker to 0 replicas before running, so old pods never see a new schema — deploy-order/version-skew risks on migrations are phantom
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`charts/lobu/files/migrate-upgrade.sh` runs as a Helm **`pre-upgrade` hook** (`charts/lobu/templates/migration-job.yaml:9`) and, whenever migrations are pending, scales **both** `*-lobu-app` and `*-lobu-worker` to `--replicas=0`, then blocks on `kubectl wait --for=delete pod` before the migration command runs. Helm only applies the new Deployments afterwards.

So there is **no version-skew window on a schema change**: no old pod is alive when the new schema lands. Do not reason about deploy ordering from `strategy.type`. Prod `summaries-app-lobu-app` *is* `RollingUpdate` with 2 replicas (the chart's `values.yaml:30` `Recreate` is overridden), and that fact is real but irrelevant here — the quiesce happens before Helm touches the Deployment at all. I flagged a skew risk on #2846 from the RollingUpdate spec alone and was wrong; a reviewer caught it.

It **fails closed**: only the pending-check's definitive "nothing pending" (exit 3 = `CHECK_PENDING_NONE_EXIT` in `scripts/migrate-up.mjs`) skips the quiesce. An unset check, a crash, or any other status still quiesces.

**Why:** this inverts the usual expand/contract instinct. A backward-incompatible index or column swap does not need a two-phase rollout here, because the only clients are gone. What it costs instead is **downtime** for the length of the migration — the ingress answers 503 — so the real question on a migration PR is "how long does this take," not "what do old pods see."

**How to apply:** on any migration PR, skip the skew analysis and size the downtime instead. Measure the target table first (`pg_total_relation_size`, live row count) — `entity_identities` at 8,204 live rows / 4 MB makes a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` sub-second, i.e. free next to the pod restart. A large table is where this actually bites. Note `CONCURRENTLY` is still correct to write (it satisfies squawk's lock-safety lint, see [[reference-on-conflict-cannot-infer-a-parameterized-expression-index]] work on #2846) even though the quiesce means nothing is contending.

Related: [[reference-deployed-prod-sha-from-image-tag]], [[reference-prod-db-read-only-query-recipe]].

cd /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu && cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-burakemre-Code-lobu/30a3648b-457b-4a87-8c17-d28e38054e73/scratchpad/iss1.md <<'EOF'
#2846 added `scope_connection_id` to `entity_identities` so a connector can declare an identity namespace connection-scoped, keeping `CARI-001` in two ERP tenants as two entities. The unique index enforces that on the write path.

The **merge-candidate resolver does not know about scope**, so it can undo it.

`packages/server/src/entity-resolution/identities.ts:24` — `loadLiveEntityIdentities` selects only `entity_id, namespace, identifier`:

```sql
SELECT entity_id, namespace, identifier
FROM entity_identities
WHERE organization_id = ...
  AND entity_id = ANY(...)
  AND deleted_at IS NULL
```

and `ResolutionIdentity` (`entity-resolution/policy.ts:26`) carries only `{namespace, identifier}`. Two entities that the new column deliberately kept apart therefore present *identical* identity evidence to the resolution policy, and an `exact` rule on that namespace sees them as the same thing.

Net effect once a connector declares `scope: 'connection'`: the write path keeps the two tenants' customers separate, and the merge path proposes joining them back together. That is precisely the collapse the column exists to prevent.

### Fix

Select `scope_connection_id` alongside namespace/identifier and carry it on `ResolutionIdentity`, so evidence only counts as `exact` when the scope keys also agree.

### Severity / timing

**Inert today** — no connector declares `scope: 'connection'`, so every live row has `scope_connection_id IS NULL` and all comparisons agree trivially. This has the same trigger condition as #2849 and must be fixed **before the first connection-scoped connector ships**, not after.

Found by the review gate on #2846 (0 blockers; this was a suggested fix). Verified by reading the query and the type, not taken on the reviewer's word.

Related: #2798, #2847, #2848, #2849.
EOF

Owner interview 2026-08-16. **Read this before re-designing connector edges.**

## DECIDED by the owner
- **Schema is ORG-owned.** Connectors reference entity types and relationship
  types BY NAME and never create them. `lobu apply` already manages both
  (`packages/cli/src/commands/_lib/apply/client.ts`). This kills #2804 as a
  feature — it becomes "make the missing-type failure loud".
- **Manifest shape**: reference attributions by NAME, do not redeclare endpoints
  ([[reference_connector_edges_reuse_attributions_not_a_new_resolver]]).
- **ACL types**: deny first, grants later
  ([[reference_connector_declared_edges_acl_hole]]).
- **Milestone that matters: Prodma / ERP end to end.** Not breadth, not the
  general platform.
- **Who writes connectors**: first-party, PLUS customers authoring their own
  *with their coding agents*, plus eventually some public exposure. The realistic
  threat is therefore **an agent writing a plausible-but-wrong manifest**, not a
  malicious publisher. Publisher trust does not mitigate it.

## The org-owned-schema decision does NOT close the ACL hole
I claimed it did; that was wrong. **Lobu creates `member_of` itself** via
`ensureMemberOfType` on any Slack or GitHub ACL sync, so the type exists in an
org without anyone authoring it, and a connector can then reference it.

`entity_relationship_types` has **no owner/system column** — only a nullable
`created_by` that platform paths pass as `NULL`. It DOES have a `metadata` jsonb,
so stamping platform-owned types needs **no migration**.

## SIZING BELOW IS SUPERSEDED — read this first
codex reviewed it and found the seam is wrong:
[[reference_connector_edges_must_write_from_afterpersist_not_attributions]].
Edges must be written from `insertEvent`'s `afterPersist`, not the attribution
transaction, which commits before any event row exists. It also argues for an
**assertion ledger** (a new table) rather than provenance in edge metadata,
because the live-triple unique index collapses two producers of the same edge
onto one row — so metadata can only name one, and disconnecting it either
deletes an edge others still assert or leaves access behind. That argument is
sound. Its bottom line: don't ship direct connector inserts into
`entity_relationships` before the assertion boundary exists.

Part 2 of connector-declared edges. Depends on the manifest surface (#2856) and must not land before the provenance boundary (#2858) — see the dissent section below.

## The seam: `afterPersist`, not the attribution transaction

The obvious place to write these edges is the attribution transaction. **That is wrong**: it commits before any event row exists, so an edge written there has nothing to point at.

Edges must be written from `insertEvent`'s `afterPersist`.

## The hard part is already done

`resolveLinksByKind` (`packages/server/src/utils/entity-link-upsert.ts:734`) already tracks `byRule` and `matchesByRule`, keyed by rule **and** item index, inside `withEntityWriteTransaction`. At the moment both endpoints are resolved, the server is holding both entity ids in the same transaction — and simply drops them.

So the write itself is small: read the manifest's `relationships`, look up the two resolved ids by rule name and item index, and call `upsertEdges` (`packages/server/src/utils/edge-writes.ts`) with them. `upsertEdges` is already the shared conflict-safe batch path for four materializers, and is idempotent by design, which is what a resync needs.

## D4 — retraction (the genuinely hard one)

An invoice's customer changes. Who removes the old edge?

`events` is append-only and a resync **supersedes** the row and mints a new `events.id` for the same source item, so identity across syncs must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key — never `events.id`.

That means "the edge set this source item currently asserts" has to be diffable across syncs. Decide and write down: is retraction a delete, a tombstone, or a superseding assertion? This interacts directly with #2858 — if two producers assert the same edge, one retracting must not remove access the other still asserts.

## D5 — cardinality

An invoice has **one** customer. Every existing relationship type is many-to-many, so there is nowhere to say that today, and every writer guesses. Tracked as #2803; this is the first consumer that actually needs it.

## D7 — provenance key

Which key identifies "this connector, this connection, this source item asserted this edge". Feeds directly into #2858.

## Do not shortcut

Do **not** ship direct connector inserts into `entity_relationships` before the assertion boundary exists. The live-triple unique index collapses two producers of the same edge onto one row, so edge metadata can only ever name one producer — and disconnecting that one either deletes an edge others still assert, or leaves access behind. Both are security-relevant.

Related: #2856, #2858, #2803, #2799, #2809.

Part 3 of connector-declared edges (#2856, #2857). This is the boundary the other two depend on, even though it ships last in build order — nothing may insert connector-declared edges into `entity_relationships` until it exists.

## The problem

`entity_relationships` has a **live-triple unique index**: one row per (from, to, type). If two producers assert the same edge — say an ACL sync and an ERP connector both saying "Alice is a member of Acme" — they collapse onto a single row.

Consequences, both bad:

- Edge metadata can name **only one** producer. Whichever wrote first owns the provenance, and the second is invisible.
- Disconnecting that producer either **deletes an edge others still assert**, or **leaves access behind**. For ACL-managed types this is a security defect, not a bookkeeping one.

Provenance in edge metadata cannot express "two independent parties assert this". The data model needs a place for N assertions behind one materialized edge.

## Shape

An **assertion ledger**: a new table recording (producer, source item, edge triple, asserted-at), with `entity_relationships` as the materialized union. Removing a producer's assertion recomputes the edge — it survives iff some other assertion still stands.

This is a **new table and a migration**, which requires owner sign-off before implementation (repo rule: never add a table or change DB design without surfacing the proposal first). The proposal exists (codex, 2026-08-16) and its argument was assessed as sound; it has not been signed off as a build.

## Why it was deferred

Deliberately deferred **until a second producer exists**. With one producer, the ledger is a table with exactly one row per edge and no observable benefit. Connector-declared edges (#2857) are that second producer — so this stops being theoretical the moment #2857 is real, and must land first.

## Open

D6 (provenance key) is unresolved and is the same decision as D7 in #2857 — settle it once, in one place.

Artifact with all 7 decisions and the dissent: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/852de803-ebd3-48b1-b680-6bf7c9852b14

Related: #2856, #2857, #2799, #2809.
EOF

Reproduced 2026-08-17 with a passing CONTROL that isolates the cause. Test:
`packages/server/src/__tests__/integration/authz/spike-approval-hold-vs-invariant.test.ts`

## The sequence

1. invoice in `draft`; spec is `issued: { to:["posted"], frozen:true,
   writableOnExit:{ posted:["einvoice_uuid"] } }`
2. a HUMAN moves `draft → issued` — legal, and claims ownership of `status`
3. an AGENT writes `{ status:"posted", einvoice_uuid:"…" }` — the legal exit plus
   the one field `writableOnExit` permits
4. the gate holds `status` (human-owned), `computeFieldMerge` STRIPS it
5. effective patch = `{ einvoice_uuid }` with NO transition → frozen state,
   non-exempt field → **DENY**

**CONTROL passes:** the identical agent write SUCCEEDS when no human owns
`status`. So the cause is the ownership hold, not the rule.

## Why it is worse than a failed write

- The error says `frozen in state "issued": cannot write einvoice_uuid`. That is
  NOT the real cause (an approval hold on a different field). Misdiagnosed.
- **The approval card is never created.** `entity-management.ts:1134` returns from
  inside the tx; the deferral is built at `:1142`–`:1147` AFTER it. The throw
  skips it. So the agent's work is denied AND dropped with no pending record.

## The general principle

Partial field commits and cross-field invariants are **logically incompatible** —
committing a subset of a consistent set can produce an inconsistent state. Any
system with both must pick. Today Lobu picks silently-lose-the-write.

**Recommended fix:** when a type has a `check`, an approval hold becomes
ALL-OR-NOTHING — defer the whole write rather than partially commit. The
alternative (pass `pending: string[]` into ctx so rules can skip held fields)

A deny throws → the transaction rolls back → anything written inside it disappears. And the audit is post-commit anyway, so it never runs at all. Same shape as the lost approval card in #2860.

**So you get a diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing when it did.** That is exactly backwards for an audit trail: the interesting events are the refusals.

## Why this gates write rules

Adding write rules makes it materially worse. Every `deny` becomes a silent failure — and #2860 proves a denial can be **wrong** as well as invisible. Shipping rules on top of an audit trail that cannot record refusals means a misattributed denial leaves no trace to debug from.

**Auditing denials is a prerequisite for shipping rules, not a follow-up.**

## Implementation

Write the audit event **after** the rollback, on a **fresh connection** — the rolled-back transaction cannot carry it. This is the one place where a separate connection is correct rather than a smell, and it should carry a comment saying so.

Then close the coverage gaps: create, delete, merge, link/unlink/update_link.

Also decide what "dropped after retry" should do. A `void`, un-awaited audit write that logs and moves on is fine for a nice-to-have diff and not fine for a compliance record; if the trail is load-bearing, the drop needs to surface somewhere a human sees.

Related: #2859, #2860.
EOF

Running server integration files locally with `bunx vitest` executes them **concurrently against one database**. One file's `beforeEach(cleanupTestDatabase)` truncates another file's fixtures mid-test, which surfaces as convincing but entirely fake failures:

#2846 is merged and everything outstanding is now on GitHub rather than in this session's context.

## Merged

`70e5abae1` — identity scope, 16 files, +609/−65. All 10 required contexts reported and passed before `--admin`; review returned **0 blockers** (bug_free 88, tests adequate); ui-review not applicable.

Two things I corrected along the way:

**The rollout risk you accepted doesn't exist.** `charts/lobu/files/migrate-upgrade.sh` is a `pre-upgrade` hook that scales app *and* worker to 0 and waits `--for=delete` before migrating, failing closed. Old pods are gone before the index swap. I'd reasoned from `RollingUpdate` on the Deployment, which is true but never applies. Correction posted on the PR. The replacement concern — quiesce downtime — I measured rather than assumed: 8,204 live rows / 4 MB, so a `CONCURRENTLY` build is sub-second.

**The PR body claimed 3 tests; it's 4.** Re-ran (4 passed), fixed the body, flagged that the mutation transcript predates the fourth test.

**Identity scope follow-ups** — #2847, #2848, #2849, #2850, #2852. Short answer: the split isn't by size, it's by **whether a failing gate catches the mistake**. This repo has unusually strong gates — `make pre-pr-remote`, `make review`, CI with 16 jobs. Where correctness is testable, a weaker model is fine because the gate will stop it. Where the failure is silent or the decision is a judgment call, a weaker model produces something plausible and wrong, and nothing catches it.

By that axis:

## Safe to delegate (gate catches errors)

**#2852** — one doc-comment line. ~15 min. Only ask: confirm the inverted-default claim before writing it.

**#2862** — either a docs paragraph or ~20 lines asserting the test setup is running under `singleFork`. Self-verifying.

**#2851** — Owletto `acl_managed`. ~100 lines: add a required field to `EntityRelationshipRow`, gate the controls, test. The *code* is easy. The cost is the hosted before/after artifact `ui-review` demands when the diff touches `src/` — that's fiddly and has burned sessions before. Delegate the code, expect to help with the proof.

**#2864** — prod verification. Mechanical queries, no design. Needs care, not capability: the trap is reading a truncated result and concluding absence. The issue already spells out the exact queries.

## Delegate with a strong reviewer

**#2850** — small code (add `scope_connection_id` to one SELECT, one type, one comparison, ~30 lines) but it sits in merge semantics. A weak model will likely write it correctly and won't notice if it breaks an existing merge path.

**#2847** — manifest-load validation, ~50–80 lines. Well-bounded.

**#2853** — output is a written re-scope, not code. Low risk, but the whole value is judgment, so a weak model gives you a summary of the issue text back.

**#2859** — the code is already written (1,031 insertions on `feat/entity-transitions`). The lift is push, PR, and survive review cycles. Mechanical, but each cycle is ~15+ min of gate time, so a model that iterates blindly burns a lot of wall-clock.

## Don't delegate — these are decisions, not implementations

**#2849, #2848** — both are "what's the stable key / what happens to existing rows", with no obvious answer. Any model will produce a confident design; you won't be able to tell from the output whether it's right.

**#2858 + #2863's table question** — the spike argues no new table is needed, the proposal argues for one. That's a genuine disagreement to settle, and it gates #2857. Also #2858 needs your sign-off anyway since it adds a table.

**#2860, #2861** — subtle correctness in ordering and rollback semantics. #2861 in particular requires writing an audit record on a fresh connection *after* a rollback, which reads like a smell and is the correct answer; a weak model will "fix" it by moving the call and lose the record silently.

**#2854** — deceptively small. The fix is ~10 lines. The work is making a flaky test fail *reliably* first. A weaker model will widen the timeout, see green, and declare it fixed — which is exactly the outcome the issue warns against.

**#2855** — mechanical-looking, genuinely dangerous. Conflict resolution here has dropped 1000+ lines via the web UI, and both directions have failure modes (main's side loses features, the branch's side reverts merged fixes). Every hunk needs a read.

## What I'd actually do

Give opencode the first tier plus #2847 and #2850 — that's five or six real PRs of genuine progress with the gates as a safety net. Keep #2849/#2848/#2858 for a decision session with me or whoever owns the design; they're blocked on choices, not on hands, so throwing capacity at them just generates plausible answers you'd have to audit anyway.

The write-rules cluster (#2859–#2861) I'd treat as one focused piece of work rather than three delegated tickets — the blockers are the interesting part and they interact.

content.text: Both closed. Now the interview — these are the four that actually block work, and they're all decisions no amount of implementation effort resolves.

questions.question: #2849: connection-scoped identities key on `connections.id`, so deleting and re-creating a connection re-mints every entity as a duplicate. Reconnecting is routine, so this generates bad prod data the first time an ERP connector ships. What should scope actually key on?

options.label: Connector declares a tenant key
options.description: The manifest names the field carrying the tenant/workspace identity (e.g. the ERP tenant id). Semantically correct: what distinguishes two tenants is the tenant, not our row. Survives reconnect, and correctly collapses two connections to the SAME tenant. Costs a new declared surface and fails loudly if a connector omits it.

options.label: Make reconnect reuse the row
options.description: Fix at the source: reconnecting soft-deletes/restores the existing `connections` row instead of creating a new id. Much smaller change, no SDK surface, no migration to the index. But it only fixes reconnect — two connections to the same tenant still fork, and it makes connection identity load-bearing in a way it isn't today.
options.preview:
reconnect flow:
  BEFORE: DELETE connection -> INSERT (new id)
  AFTER:  UPDATE connections SET deleted_at=NULL
          WHERE org=? AND connector_key=?
            AND external_ref=?

scope_connection_id unchanged

options.label: Auto-derive from auth
options.description: Server derives the scope key at auth time from (connector_key + the external workspace/account id the provider returns). No manifest change — connectors get it for free. But it only works where the provider exposes a stable external id, and it is invisible to the connector author, so when it is wrong there is nothing to inspect.

options.label: Accept and heal
options.description: Let the re-mint happen and rely on the merge path to reunite the duplicates afterwards. Cheapest now. Given #2850 (the merge resolver is scope-blind) this currently means duplicates get merged back by the very path that ignores scope — so it is the option most likely to produce a mess.

questions.question: #2861: rules shipped in #2842, so denials are happening now and none are recorded — successful updates get a field-level diff, every refusal is invisible. What shape should the denial record take?

options.label: Record every denial, post-rollback
options.description: After the transaction rolls back, write the audit event on a fresh connection. Captures the refusal, the rule that fired, and the proposal. Reads like a smell (a second connection) and is the correct answer — it needs a comment saying so. Highest fidelity; also the most work.

options.label: Rule denials only
options.description: Record refusals that came from a per-type rule, but not permission/ownership holds (those already produce approval cards, so there is a record elsewhere). Narrower and cheaper, and arguably the holds are not 'denials' at all. Risk: the two look identical to a user debugging, and the split is invisible from the outside.

options.label: Structured log + metrics
options.description: Emit denials to the log stream and a counter rather than the events table. Cheapest, no schema change, good enough to answer 'are we denying a lot suddenly'. Not a record: not queryable per entity, not retained, and useless for 'why was this specific write refused three weeks ago'.

options.label: Leave it for now
options.description: Rules are new and denial volume is unknown. Wait until something actually goes wrong before designing the record. Honest option, but it means the first incident is the one with no data.

questions.question: #2858 proposes an assertion ledger as a new table; the spike's final commit (#2863) claims connector-declared edges need no new table. That contradiction gates the whole edge write path (#2857). How do you want it settled?

options.label: Read the spike's evidence first
options.description: Before either is built: have someone read `edge-claims-spike.ts` (287 lines) and its tests against the ledger proposal and report which claim survives. This is a real question about whether one row per edge can carry N producers, and the spike has 193 lines of tests asserting it can. Cheap to answer, and both other options are guesses until it is answered.

options.label: New ledger table — sign off now
options.description: Take the proposal: a table of (producer, source item, edge triple, asserted-at), with `entity_relationships` as the materialized union. Removing one producer's assertion recomputes the edge. Clean model, unblocks #2857 immediately. Costs a table and a migration, and would make the spike's 3095 lines partly wasted.

options.label: No new table — adopt the spike
options.description: Trust the spike's proof and build claims on existing storage. Cheapest path and reuses working prototype code. Risk: the live-triple unique index genuinely does collapse two producers onto one row, so if the spike's approach papers over that rather than solving it, the failure mode is ACL access left behind after a disconnect.

questions.question: #2857 D4: an invoice's customer changes. `events` is append-only and a resync mints new event ids, so the server needs some way to know an edge is no longer asserted. What is the retraction model?

options.label: Full re-assert + diff
options.description: Each sync declares the COMPLETE edge set for a source item; the server diffs against what that item asserted last time and retracts the difference. No new manifest concept, idempotent, and matches how the sync path already works. Requires a stable per-source-item key (origin_id, not events.id) and means a partial sync must never look like a full one.

options.label: Explicit retraction
options.description: The connector says what to remove. Precise and handles partial syncs safely. But it puts the burden on manifest authors — who are increasingly coding agents — to remember the negative case, and forgetting it fails silently by leaving stale edges (and therefore stale access) in place.

options.label: Valid-time supersede
options.description: Never delete; close the old edge's validity interval and open a new one. Full history, answers 'who was the customer in March', and folds this decision into #2801 (valid-time on edges) which is already open and awaiting your sign-off. Bigger change, and every read path then has to be time-aware or it silently sees closed edges.

options.label: No retraction in v1
options.description: Ship assertion only; edges accumulate. Acceptable if the first ERP entities are append-only in practice. Not acceptable for anything ACL-adjacent, since a stale edge is stale access — so it would need a hard rule that connector-declared edges can never touch an authorization type.

content.text:
Decision 1 has an immediate consequence worth naming: it changes the column I shipped 20 minutes ago. `scope_connection_id bigint` becomes `scope_key text`, and `EntityIdentitySpec` gains `scopeKeyPath`. That's the cheapest it will ever be — every row is still NULL and no connector declares `scope: 'connection'` yet — but it needs to happen before anything writes to that column, not after.

Second round:

questions.question: #2848: once rows exist under one scope key, changing a namespace's scope (or its `scopeKeyPath`) re-keys every identity — old rows keep the old key and new syncs mint duplicates. What should happen when a connector changes it?

options.label: Refuse until explicitly migrated
options.description: Detect the change at manifest load and hard-fail with the old and new key shown. The org then runs an explicit backfill to re-key existing rows. Nothing silently forks, and the failure names the exact cause. Costs a detection mechanism (store the declared scope shape per namespace) plus a backfill tool.
options.preview:
$ lobu apply
ERROR erp_customer: identity scope changed
  was: scope=organization
  now: scope=connection key=metadata.tenant_id
  4,182 existing identities use the old key.

Run `lobu identities rekey erp_customer` first.

options.label: Auto-backfill on change
options.description: Detect it and re-key the existing rows automatically in the same migration/apply step. Nothing for the operator to do, no forked entities. Risk: re-keying is not always well-defined — going from org-scope to connection-scope has to invent a key for rows that never had one, and it may be genuinely ambiguous which tenant an old row belonged to.

options.label: Allow it, surface the drift
options.description: Let the change through, but detect and report identities stranded under the old key so someone can reconcile. Lowest friction for connector authors iterating. Means production can sit in a forked state indefinitely, and the report is only useful if someone reads it.

options.label: Don't solve it yet
options.description: No connector declares connection scope today, so no rows can be stranded. Defer until the first one ships and we know what a real scope change looks like. Cheapest, and the failure lands on whoever ships that connector.

questions.question: #2847: scope is declared per attribution rule, not per namespace, so one connector can declare `erp_customer` connection-scoped in one event kind and org-scoped in another. Today that silently produces two entities. How should conflicting declarations resolve?

options.label: Hard fail at manifest load
options.description: A namespace gets exactly one scope per connector; two different declarations is a validation error before anything syncs. Simple rule, easy to explain, catches the agent-authored-manifest case at the earliest possible point. Means a connector cannot legitimately use one namespace two ways — which is probably correct, but forecloses it.

options.label: Hoist scope to the namespace
options.description: Move the declaration off the attribution rule entirely and onto a per-connector namespace registry, so a conflict becomes structurally impossible rather than validated against. Cleaner model and removes a whole error class. Larger SDK change, and it separates the scope from the rule that uses it, which is less readable at the call site.

options.label: First declaration wins, warn
options.description: Take the first, log the conflict. Never blocks a sync. Given manifests are increasingly written by coding agents, a warning is very likely to go unread — and the failure it is warning about is silent entity forking.

questions.question: #2801 (valid-time on edges) has been awaiting your sign-off and is still open. You just chose diff-based retraction over valid-time for connector edges, which covers the ERP case without it. Does valid-time still get built?

options.label: Not now — close or park it
options.description: Diff-based retraction answers the ERP need. Valid-time is a bigger change that makes every edge read path time-aware or subtly wrong, and there is no second use case pressing for it. Park #2801 with the reasoning recorded so it is not re-litigated from scratch.

options.label: Build it, but after the edge path lands
options.description: Keep it as the eventual model — 'who was the customer in March' is a real ERP question — but sequence it after #2856/#2857 so it is designed against a working edge writer rather than in the abstract.

options.label: Build it now, it changes the design
options.description: If edges are getting valid-time eventually, retraction should be a validity-interval close from the start rather than a delete we later migrate. Costs more now, avoids reworking the retraction path twice.

questions.question: Given all of the above, what should the delegated work (opencode) start on while the design questions settle?

options.label: The safe tier
options.description: #2852 (SDK doc line), #2862 (vitest singleFork guard), #2851 (Owletto acl_managed), #2864 (prod-verify). Well-specified, gate-verifiable, no design judgment. Roughly four small PRs.

options.label: Re-key #2846 to scope_key
options.description: Implement decision 1: `scope_connection_id bigint` → `scope_key text`, add `scopeKeyPath` to the SDK, migrate the index. Mechanical and urgent (cheapest before anything writes the column), but it touches the ON CONFLICT blast radius again — 10 sites, SQL literal not bound param.

options.label: #2850 scope-blind resolver
options.description: Small diff (add the scope column to one SELECT, one type, one comparison) but sits in merge semantics. Should be re-keyed to `scope_key` at the same time so it is not written twice.

options.label: Read the spike's evidence
options.description: Decision 3's answer: have someone read `edge-claims-spike.ts` and its tests against the ledger proposal and report which claim survives. Analysis, not code — unblocks #2857/#2858.

content.text:
You're right, and it's stronger than I'd assumed. I checked: superseding **retains** the old row — `supersedes_event_id` links the new version to its predecessor, plus a denormalized `superseded_by` inverse edge, with a partial unique index on the link. So the event log is a complete version chain, not a latest-value store. "What did this source item say at time T" is already answerable.

Three things events still don't give you, in descending order of how much they matter:

**Valid time vs transaction time.** Events record *when we learned* something. An invoice dated March but entered in August appears in the log at August. Replaying to March tells you what you knew in March, which is not what was true in March. For an ERP of record where backdating and period-close are routine, those diverge — and that's precisely the gap valid-time exists to close. But it's only a gap if you commit to backdated as-of queries, which hasn't been decided.

**Coverage.** Only connector-declared edges would derive from events. `manage_entity`, `auto-linker`, `access-graph`, `github-team-graph` and `channel-about` all write edges with no originating event, so event replay reconstructs one producer's edges, not the edge table.

**Cost.** Answering "who was the customer in March" by walking the chain is an aggregation over history — the thing your own rule forbids on a request path. You'd have to materialize it regardless, so "the data exists" and "the product can answer it" aren't the same claim.

My call: **you don't need it.** Diff-based retraction gives you current state, the event chain gives you how it got there, and nothing today asks a backdated as-of question. I'm parking #2801 with that reasoning recorded and a named trigger to revive it — backdating/period-close becoming real, or a second edge producer needing as-of reads. Say the word if you'd rather I close it outright.

Recording all seven decisions now.

cat > $S/d2849.md <<'EOF'
## DECIDED 2026-08-18 (owner): scope keys on a connector-declared tenant key, not `connections.id`

The manifest names the field carrying tenant identity. `connections.id` is replaced as the scope key:

```ts
identities: [{
  namespace: 'erp_customer',
  eventPath: 'metadata.customer_code',
  scope: 'connection',
  scopeKeyPath: 'metadata.tenant_id',   // NEW
}]
```

Storage changes from the column shipped in #2846:

```
scope_connection_id bigint  ->  scope_key text
index: (organization_id, namespace, identifier, COALESCE(scope_key, ''))
       WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
```

### Why

What distinguishes two ERP tenants is the **tenant**, not our connection row. Keying on the tenant fixes two things at once:

- **Reconnect survives.** Deleting and re-creating a connection no longer re-mints every entity, which was this issue.
- **Two connections to the same tenant correctly collapse** — which `connections.id` also got wrong, in the opposite direction.

### Do this NOW, before anything writes the column

This is the cheapest it will ever be. `scope_connection_id` shipped in #2846 twenty minutes before this decision; every row is NULL and **no connector declares `scope: 'connection'` yet**, so the change is behaviour-preserving today and gets progressively more expensive with every connection-scoped connector that ships.

### Implementation notes

- The sentinel changes from `0` to `''`. Owner interview 2026-08-18, immediately after #2846 merged. **Read this before re-designing identity scope or connector edges** — all seven are settled and recorded on the issues.

**#2846's column is being replaced.** `scope_connection_id bigint` → `scope_key text`, with a new `scopeKeyPath` on `EntityIdentitySpec` naming the field that carries tenant identity. ## The decisions

| # | decision |
|---|---|
| #2849 | scope keys on a **connector-declared tenant key**, not `connections.id` |
| #2848 | changing scope **hard-fails apply** until an explicit `lobu identities rekey` runs — auto-backfill would have to *invent* a key for org-scoped rows, sometimes with no answer in the data |

| #2858 | **read the spike's evidence first**; neither ledger nor no-table adopted |

**Superseding retains the old row.** `events.supersedes_event_id` links each version to its predecessor, with a denormalized `superseded_by` inverse edge and a partial unique index on the link. The event log is a complete version chain, not a latest-value store — so transaction-time history already exists without valid-time.

What events still do **not** give you, and the reason this is parked rather than closed:

1. **Valid time ≠ transaction time.** Events record when we *learned* it. An invoice dated March, entered in August, logs at August. For an ERP of record with backdating and period-close these diverge.
2. **Coverage** — only connector-declared edges derive from events. `manage_entity`, `auto-linker`, `access-graph`, `github-team-graph`, `channel-about` write edges with no originating event.
3. **Cost** — an as-of read by walking the chain is aggregation over history, forbidden on a request path; it would need materializing anyway.

On capability: **the gates verify code, not judgment.** That's the line. `make pre-pr-remote` runs 16 CI jobs and `make review` is semantic — a weaker model iterating against those will converge on the code tasks even if it takes extra cycles. What no gate checks is whether a conclusion is *right*.

Three items fail that test, and one of them is in your batch:

**#2858 — reading the spike's evidence.** This is the one I'd pull back. The deliverable is a judgment: does the spike genuinely solve N-producers-one-row, or paper over it. A weaker model reading 480 lines of spike plus a competing proposal will produce a confident summary that agrees with whichever it read last, and nothing will contradict it. If it's wrong the failure is ACL access left behind after a disconnect. Give this to a strong model or read it yourself.

**#2854 — the flake.** No decision touched it. The work is making it fail *reliably* before changing anything. A weaker model will widen the timeout, see green, and report success — and green is indistinguishable from fixed.

**#2855 — the rebases.** Judgment per hunk, and both directions lose real work.

Everything else is now delegable. Three traps worth handing over explicitly rather than letting them be discovered:

- **The re-key**: `ON CONFLICT` infers its arbiter by comparing parse trees, so the sentinel must be a SQL literal `''`, never a bound param. It fails *non-deterministically across suites* and reads exactly like test-isolation flake — I chased that for a while myself. Say this upfront and it costs nothing; don't, and it costs a cycle.
- **#2861**: the fresh-connection-after-rollback pattern looks like a mistake. Without a comment explaining why, a model will "clean it up" and silently delete the audit trail it was sent to build.
- **#2851**: the code is trivial; the hosted before/after artifact `ui-review` wants is the actual work.

cat > $S/b2849.md <<'EOF'
> **Status: decided, ready to implement.** Owner decision 2026-08-18. This body is the complete spec — you do not need to read the comments to start.
>
> **Do this before any connector declares `scope: 'connection'`.** Every row is NULL today and no connector declares it, so the change is behaviour-preserving right now and gets more expensive with each connection-scoped connector that ships.

## Problem

#2846 shipped `entity_identities.scope_connection_id`, keying connection-scoped identities on `connections.id`. That is the wrong key, in both directions:

- **Reconnect forks.** Deleting and re-creating a connection mints a new `connections.id`, stranding every existing scoped row and re-minting all of its entities as duplicates. Reconnecting is routine, so this produces bad prod data — not a bad test.
- **Two connections to one tenant also fork.** Two connections pointing at the *same* ERP tenant should collapse onto one entity, and keying on the connection row splits them.

What actually distinguishes two ERP tenants is the **tenant**, not our connection row.

## Decision

The connector declares the field carrying tenant identity.

```ts
identities: [{
  namespace: 'erp_customer',
  eventPath: 'metadata.customer_code',
  scope: 'connection',
  scopeKeyPath: 'metadata.tenant_id',   // NEW
}]
```

Storage:

```
scope_connection_id bigint  ->  scope_key text
index: (organization_id, namespace, identifier, COALESCE(scope_key, ''))
       WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
```

## Implementation

**1. SDK** — `packages/connector-sdk/src/connector-types.ts`. Add `scopeKeyPath?: string` to `EntityIdentitySpec`. A `scope: 'connection'` declaration **without** `scopeKeyPath` must fail loudly at manifest load — never silently fall back to org scope. Silently widening scope is the exact collapse this column exists to prevent.

**2. Migration** — replace the index from #2846 (`db/migrations/20260818000000_entity_identity_connection_scope.sql` is the shipped one; write a new forward migration, do not edit it).

Follow the same pattern that one used, and re-read it before writing:
- `-- migrate:up transaction:false`
- inline the INVALID-carcass heal `DO` block so it re-runs on retry (a crashed `CONCURRENTLY` build leaves an INVALID index that `IF NOT EXISTS` would silently no-op over, recording the migration as applied with a **non-enforcing** arbiter — a silent uniqueness hole on identity claims)
- `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS` under a **new** name, then `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS` the old one
- squawk runs in CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `npx squawk-cli@2.58.0 --exclude=ban-drop-column,require-timeout-settings`). Verify locally before pushing — a plain DROP+CREATE gets 6 lock-safety findings and fails the required `migrations` check.

**3. Sentinel — the trap that will cost you a cycle if you skip this.** The sentinel becomes `''` and **must be a SQL literal**, never a bound param:

```sql
-- WRONG: never matches the index
ON CONFLICT (organization_id, namespace, identifier, COALESCE(scope_key, ${SENTINEL}))
-- RIGHT
ON CONFLICT (organization_id, namespace, identifier, COALESCE(scope_key, ''))
```

`ON CONFLICT` infers its arbiter by comparing **parse trees**. A bound `Param` never equals the index's `Const`, so it fails with *"there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification"* — **non-deterministically across suites**, which reads exactly like test-isolation flake. Do not go looking for a test-isolation bug.

**4. Blast radius.** Changing the unique index breaks **every** `ON CONFLICT` naming the old column list. That was **10 sites** in #2846 — `save_content`, `subject-identities` (×2), `canvas-events`, `promote-keyed-entities`, `member-entity`, `eval-cases`, plus 3 in test fixtures. Re-grep rather than trusting that count; fix all in one pass.

**5. Normalize `undefined`.** #2846 shipped a bug where `scopeConnectionId: undefined` reached the array literal as `String(undefined)` and Postgres rejected `invalid input syntax for type bigint: "undefined"`. Callers outside the attribution path (`resolveSenderIdentity`, tests) hand-build identities and legitimately mean org scope. Keep the field optional with `?? null` normalization. **The compiler will not catch this** — `packages/server/tsconfig` excludes `__tests__`.

**6. Fold in #2850** — the merge-candidate resolver is scope-blind. Re-key and fix it in the same pass or the same small change gets written twice.

## Test plan

- Port `packages/server/src/__tests__/integration/connectors/identity-connection-scope.test.ts` (4 tests) to `scope_key`. It already covers: scoped stays split, org-scoped still collapses, re-sync idempotent, no-connection falls back to org scope.
- Add: two connections to the **same** tenant key collapse onto one entity. This is the case `connections.id` got wrong and the whole reason for the change.
- Add: `scope: 'connection'` without `scopeKeyPath` fails at manifest load.
- Run the **bun** suites too, not just vitest — #2846 shipped a broken `toEqual` shape assertion in `gateway/connections/__tests__/sender-identity.test.ts` that a vitest-only sweep never ran.

## Verification

`bunx vitest` does **not** honour `singleFork` and will fabricate cross-file failures (#2862). Use the CI invocation:

```
cd packages/server
node ../../node_modules/.bin/vitest run <path>
```

Related: #2798, #2846, #2847, #2848, #2850.

> **Status: decided, ready to implement — but implement it inside #2849, not on its own.** Owner decision 2026-08-18.

## Problem

#2846 added scoped identities so a connector can keep `CARI-001` in two ERP tenants as two entities. The unique index enforces that on the **write** path.

The **merge-candidate resolver does not know about scope**, so it can undo it.

`packages/server/src/entity-resolution/identities.ts:24` — `loadLiveEntityIdentities` selects only three columns:

```sql
SELECT entity_id, namespace, identifier
FROM entity_identities
WHERE organization_id = ...
  AND entity_id = ANY(...)
  AND deleted_at IS NULL
```

and `ResolutionIdentity` (`entity-resolution/policy.ts:26`) carries only `{ namespace, identifier }`.

Two entities the scope key deliberately kept apart therefore present **identical** identity evidence to the resolution policy, and an `exact` rule on that namespace treats them as the same thing.

Net effect once a connector declares connection scope: the write path keeps two tenants' customers separate, and the merge path proposes joining them back together — precisely the collapse the column exists to prevent.

## Fix

Select the scope column alongside namespace/identifier, carry it on `ResolutionIdentity`, and require the scope keys to **agree** before evidence counts as `exact`.

## Implement this as part of #2849

#2849 replaces `scope_connection_id bigint` with `scope_key text`. Writing this fix against the old column and migrating it afterwards means doing the same small change twice. Do them in one pass.

## Test plan

- Two entities under different scope keys, same `(namespace, identifier)`: must **not** be proposed as a merge candidate.
- Two entities under the **same** scope key, same `(namespace, identifier)`: must still be proposed — this is the existing behaviour and the regression risk.
- Org-scoped rows (`scope_key IS NULL`) must behave exactly as they do today. Every production row is currently in this state, so a regression here is a live defect rather than a latent one.

## Severity

**Inert until a connector declares connection scope** — every live row has a NULL scope key today, so all comparisons agree trivially. Same trigger condition as #2849; both must be fixed before the first connection-scoped connector ships.

Found by the review gate on #2846 as a suggested fix, then verified by reading the query and the type rather than taken on the reviewer's word.

Related: #2798, #2846, #2849.

cat > $S/b2847.md <<'EOF'
> **Status: decided, ready to implement.** Owner decision 2026-08-18: **hard fail at manifest load.**

## Problem

Identity scope is declared per **attribution rule**, not per namespace. One connector can therefore declare `erp_customer` connection-scoped in one event kind and org-scoped in another:

```ts
// eventKinds.customer
identities: [{ namespace: 'erp_customer', eventPath: '...', scope: 'connection' }]

// eventKinds.invoice — same namespace, different scope
identities: [{ namespace: 'erp_customer', eventPath: '...' }]   // defaults to organization
```

Today this is accepted and silently produces **two entities** for the same customer. There is no validation.

## Decision

A namespace gets exactly one scope per connector. Two differing declarations for the same namespace is a **validation error before anything syncs** — not a warning, not a precedence rule.

### Why not "first declaration wins, warn"

The realistic threat is not a malicious publisher; it is **an agent authoring a plausible-but-wrong manifest**, since connectors are increasingly written by coding agents. A warning is very likely to go unread, and the thing it warns about — silent entity forking — stays invisible until someone notices duplicate customers in production.

### Accepted tradeoff

A connector cannot legitimately use one namespace two ways. That is almost certainly correct: a namespace either names something globally meaningful or it does not. Taken deliberately. If a real case for per-usage scope appears, the escape hatch is hoisting scope onto a per-connector namespace registry, which makes conflicts structurally impossible rather than merely validated.

## Implementation

Validate at manifest load. With #2849, `scopeKeyPath` is part of the declaration, so **two declarations differing only in key path are also a conflict**.

The error must name:
- the namespace
- both declared scopes (including key paths)
- the event kinds each came from

A bare "scope conflict" is not actionable — the author needs to know which two declarations to reconcile.

## Test plan

- Same namespace, two different `scope` values → load fails, error names both event kinds.
- Same namespace, same scope, different `scopeKeyPath` → load fails.
- Same namespace declared identically in two event kinds → loads fine. This is normal and must not regress.

## Depends on

#2849 (`scopeKeyPath` must exist before it can be part of the conflict check).

Related: #2798, #2848.

> **Status: decided, ready to implement.** Owner decision 2026-08-18: **refuse the change until an explicit re-key has run.**

## Problem

Once identities exist under one scope key, changing a namespace's scope — or its `scopeKeyPath` (#2849) — re-keys every future write. Existing rows keep the old key, new syncs mint duplicates under the new one, and the same customer forks into two entities. Nothing errors.

## Decision

Detect the change at manifest load and **hard-fail**, naming both shapes and the affected row count:

```
$ lobu apply
ERROR erp_customer: identity scope changed
  was: scope=organization
  now: scope=connection key=metadata.tenant_id
  4,182 existing identities use the old key.

Run `lobu identities rekey erp_customer` first.
```

The org then runs an explicit backfill to re-key existing rows.

### Why not auto-backfill

Re-keying is **not always well-defined**. Going from org scope to connection scope has to *invent* a key for rows that never had one, and which tenant an old row belonged to may be genuinely unanswerable from the data. An automatic backfill would have to guess, silently, on the identity table. Refusing and making a human choose is the correct failure.

## Implementation

**1. Persist the declared scope shape** per `(connector, namespace)` so a change is detectable at all. This does not exist today and is the bulk of the work. It needs to survive connector version bumps, since that is exactly when the shape changes.

**2. The error must be actionable** — old shape, new shape, affected count. Counting requires a query against `entity_identities` scoped to that namespace; keep it off any request path (it belongs in apply/preflight, which is allowed to aggregate).

**3. New CLI command** `lobu identities rekey <namespace>`.

**Publish `@lobu/cli` BEFORE the server change that starts rejecting apply.** The CLI is public on npm, and a server that fails closed against an older CLI locks orgs out of their own apply — they would get the error with no `rekey` command available to satisfy it. Publish is dispatch-only and gated on `app-image-smoke`.

## Test plan

- Namespace declared org-scoped, rows exist, manifest changes to connection-scoped → apply fails, error names both shapes and the true row count.
- Same change with **zero** existing rows → apply succeeds. Nothing is stranded, so there is nothing to refuse.
- `scopeKeyPath` changed while `scope` stays `connection` → also fails. The key is what re-keys, not the scope word.
- After `rekey`, apply succeeds and existing rows carry the new key.

## Depends on

#2849 (`scope_key` / `scopeKeyPath` must exist first).

Related: #2798, #2847.

cat > $S/b2861.md <<'EOF'
> **Status: decided, ready to implement.** Owner decision 2026-08-18.
>
> **This is live debt, not a prerequisite.** It was filed as a blocker for shipping write rules. #2842 shipped them (`006f3c568`, merged 2026-08-18T00:10:12Z), so denials are being produced in production **right now** and none are recorded.

## Problem

| what happened | audited? |
|---|---|
| successful UPDATE | yes — field-level diff, `manage_entity.ts:585` |
| successful CREATE | **no** — `handleCreate:271` never calls it |
| delete / merge / link / unlink / update_link | **no** — `:1365`, `:675`, `:1737` |
| **DENIED write** | **no — structurally** |
| the audit write itself failing | **dropped** |

You get a diff when nothing went wrong, and nothing when it did. For an audit trail that is exactly backwards — the interesting events are the refusals.

### Why denials are structurally invisible

A deny throws → the transaction rolls back → anything written inside it disappears. The audit is post-commit anyway, so it never runs.

`recordChangeEvent` (`insert-event.ts:756`) returns `void`, is **not awaited**, and its `.catch` at `:775` logs:

```
change audit event DROPPED after retry — audit trail is missing this row
```

## Decision

Record **every** denial, after the rollback, on a fresh connection:

```ts
try {
  await tx(...)          // throws on deny
} catch (e) {
  if (isDenial(e)) {
    // fresh conn: the tx that would carry
    // this record is already rolled back
    await recordDenial(freshConn, {...})
  }
  throw e
}
```

Capture the refusal, the rule that fired, and the proposal that was refused.

### The fresh connection is correct — say so in a comment

It looks like a mistake. It is the only way to keep the row: the transaction that produced the denial no longer exists. **Without a comment at the call site, the next reader will "clean it up" and silently delete the audit trail.**

## Also in scope

Close the coverage gaps: create, delete, merge, link/unlink/update_link.

## Open sub-question (decide during implementation)

Fire-and-forget is defensible for a nice-to-have diff and not for a record someone relies on. Decide whether a **dropped denial record** must surface somewhere a human sees, rather than logging and moving on. Recommend it does — a denial that vanished is indistinguishable from a write that never happened.

## Test plan

- A rule denial produces a persisted record naming the rule and the proposal, **after** the write rolled back.
- Assert on the **persisted** row, not a hand-built object. A test that builds the record itself passes with the produce→persist plumbing severed.
- The entity itself is unchanged — the rollback still rolled back.
- Create / delete / merge / link each produce a record on success.

Related: #2842, #2859 (closed as superseded).
